script:
### Open

You're in the middle of a ticket in Jira, and a Slack message comes in.

You answer it, then you see an email and reply to that too.

Then you go back to the ticket, and you have to read it again to remember where you were.

For a lot of us, that's a normal workday, with a few more apps and a lot of browser tabs in between.

That switching between apps costs a lot more than it looks like, and it's very close to what my master's thesis is about.

So in this video, I'll show you what the research says that cost is, why nobody sees it, and what you and your company can do about it.

### How often we switch between apps at work

So how often do people actually switch between apps at work?

In 2022, Harvard Business Review published a study where the researchers tracked 137 people, in 20 teams, across three Fortune 500 companies, for up to five weeks.

Most of them worked in back-office teams, like finance, HR and supply chain.

On average, each person toggled between apps and websites nearly 1,200 times a day.

If you've watched my video on task switching, you've heard that number before.

So I want to show you two other numbers from the same study, because they say a lot about the tools.

The first one is about one supply chain task at a big consumer goods company.

To get that single task done, each person involved switched about 350 times, between 22 different apps and websites.

*[on screen: one task / 22 apps and websites / about 350 switches]*

And over a full day, one employee there toggled more than 3,600 times.

The second number is this one.

After 65% of switches, people moved to yet another app in less than 11 seconds.

So they'd open an app, spend a few seconds there, and leave again.

The researchers wrote something about these workers that I keep thinking about.

They said, "A sizable part of their jobs is to act as the glue between disparate applications."

Disparate here means apps that don't connect to each other.

So the person becomes the connection.

You copy an order number from one system, paste it into another one, check a third one to confirm it went through, and send a message about it in a fourth.

One small note, because I'm a researcher and I care about this.

This was published as an article in a business magazine, so it wasn't peer-reviewed like an academic paper.

But academic research on switching at work points the same way, and I'll show you some of it in this video.

### What you reload when you switch apps

Every time you switch apps at work, you have to reload your context.

Your context is everything you were holding in your head for the task you were doing.

Take a developer's day as an example.

You're fixing a bug from a Jira ticket.

In your head, you're holding which file you were in, which test was failing, what you already tried, and what you were going to try next.

Then Slack pings, and someone needs a quick answer about a different feature.

To answer them, you load a whole different context. Which feature they mean, what that code does, and what you told them about it last week.

Then you go back to the bug, and the first context has to come back.

You read the ticket again. You find the right tab. You scroll back to where you were in the file. And you try to remember what you were going to try next.

*[on screen: what you reload / the task / where you stopped / what you already tried / what comes next]*

In the Harvard Business Review study, the cost of each switch was a little over two seconds.

That's the extra time people needed to get going on the next step after they switched.

Two seconds sounds like nothing.

But across nearly 1,200 switches a day, they worked out that it came to just under four hours a week.

That's about five working weeks a year, or 9% of their time at work.

*[on screen: ~2 seconds a switch / just under 4 hours a week / ~9% of the working year]*

And two seconds is only the part that shows up on the screen.

The part in your head takes longer, and it has a name. It's called attention residue.

Sophie Leroy, a researcher who studies how people work, showed in 2009 that when you move from one task to another, part of your attention stays on the first task.

And in her studies, it was stronger when people left the first task unfinished.

That's most app switches at work, because a Slack message doesn't wait for you to finish your ticket.

### Why your work looks fine but you feel exhausted

There's a study I think explains why switching and interruptions can leave you exhausted, while your work still looks fine.

It's from 2008, by Gloria Mark and her colleagues, and the title is "The cost of interrupted work: more speed and stress."

They gave people an email task to do, and some of them kept getting interrupted while they worked.

The people who got interrupted finished in less time, and the quality of their work didn't drop.

So if you only looked at the work, the interruptions did no harm.

But when the researchers asked people how they felt, the ones who got interrupted reported more stress, more frustration, more time pressure and more effort.

*[on screen: interrupted people / finished faster, same quality / more stress, frustration, time pressure, effort]*

The researchers think people make up for interruptions by working faster, and they pay for it in stress.

So the output stays the same, and the cost moves into the person.

That study was about interruptions, which isn't exactly the same as switching apps.

But at work, a lot of app switching starts with an interruption. A ping, a notification, a little red badge on your email.

And Microsoft's 2025 Work Trend Index looked at activity across Microsoft 365 and found that during core work hours, the average person got interrupted about every two minutes, by a meeting, an email or a chat message.

That's around 275 interruptions a day.

So if your day feels like it's made of other people's pings, the numbers back you up.

### Why the cost of app switching is invisible

So why does nobody see the cost of switching between apps at work?

I think there are four reasons.

The first reason is that each switch is tiny.

Two seconds here, one quick reply there. Nobody writes any of that down.

The second reason is that every app only sees itself.

Slack can tell your company how many messages you sent. Jira can tell them how many tickets you closed.

But none of them can see the time you spent between them, getting from one app to another and finding your place again.

*[on screen: Slack sees messages / Jira sees tickets / nobody sees the gaps in between]*

The third reason has a name in my field. It's called articulation work.

Two researchers, Susan Leigh Star and Anselm Strauss, wrote about it in 1999.

Articulation work is all the coordinating you do so that the main work can happen.

Keeping track of who's doing what, lining things up, and making sure the pieces fit together.

And one thing they pointed out is that this kind of work is often invisible.

It doesn't show up as a result, and people usually only notice it when it's missing, when something falls through the cracks.

Being the glue between your apps is that kind of work.

The fourth reason comes from Gloria Mark's interruption study from 2008.

People can keep their output the same by working faster, so the cost shows up as stress, inside the person, where no report looks.

This is the part that's closest to my thesis.

I'm doing my master's in Human-Computer Interaction at Tallinn University, and my thesis is on the invisible cognitive cost of switching between productivity tools.

I'm in my second year, and my plan is to finish my other courses this autumn, so spring 2027 is just the thesis.

So to be clear, everything in this video comes from published research. None of it is from my own thesis results.

What I can tell you is why I care about it.

I think most workplace tools get designed and measured one at a time, while people work across all of them at once.

So the cost lands in the gaps between the tools, and it's nobody's job to look there.

And that's where the fixes come in, some on your company's side and some on yours.

### What companies can do about app switching

A lot of app switching at work comes from how the work is set up, so a big part of the fix sits with the company. The team lead, the manager, and whoever picks the tools.

The researchers behind the Harvard Business Review study gave some suggestions, so I'll start with theirs.

First, count the cost of every new app.

Their words were, "Rationalize the cost of introducing new applications."

Every new tool is one more place to check, and one more place where things can get lost.

So before adding one, I would ask what it replaces.

Second, they suggest approving new software "with actual hands-on users."

The person who buys a tool is often not the person who'll be switching into it all day.

Third, rebalance the work.

They noted that people whose jobs involve constantly switching between apps are more likely to get bored and distracted, and more likely to leave.

So they suggest spreading that kind of work across the team, so it doesn't all land on the same few people.

*[optional line: And the next two are my own, and they're the ones I'd push for first.]*

Next, decide where each kind of thing lives.

For example, decisions go in the ticket. Quick questions go in Slack. Anything that needs a proper reply goes in email.

So if a decision gets made in a Slack thread, someone writes it in the Jira ticket, and the next person doesn't have to search three apps to find it.

When the whole team uses each tool the same way, people can stop checking everything just in case.

Then, agree on how fast people need to reply.

If everyone believes a Slack message needs an answer in two minutes, everyone keeps Slack open and keeps switching to it.

If the team agrees that a couple of hours is fine for anything that isn't urgent, people can close it for a while and get on with their work.

There's a small study from 2012, by Gloria Mark and her colleagues, where they cut a group of office workers off from email for five working days.

Without email, people switched between windows less often, they stayed on each task longer, and heart rate monitors showed they were less stressed.

It was a small study, so I wouldn't tell your company to ban email.

But it shows that how your tools are set up changes how much you switch.

### How to reduce app switching at work yourself

If you can't change the tools at your job, there are still things you can do to reduce app switching yourself.

The first one is to get to a stopping point before you switch.

Attention residue is stronger when you leave a task unfinished.

So if you can take one more minute to finish the sentence you're writing or the test you're running, do that, and then go and answer the message.

The second one is to leave yourself a note before you switch.

In my video on task switching, I said I leave myself a one-line note about where I stopped and what comes next.

It turns out there's research on exactly this.

In 2018, Sophie Leroy and Theresa Glomb tested what they called a "ready-to-resume plan."

Before switching, people took a moment to write down where they were in the task and what they'd do when they came back.

And that plan reduced attention residue, and people did better on the task they switched to.

*[on screen: a ready-to-resume note / "BOOK-142: order total is wrong when a discount is applied. Tried the rounding fix, didn't work. Next: check the tax step."]*

So your note helps the thing you're coming back to, and it also helps the thing you're switching to.

The third one is to check Slack and email at set times.

I batch my replies, so I pay the switching cost once, instead of every time a message lands.

You can do it every hour, or whatever your job allows, and keep notifications off in between.

The fourth one is to keep open only what the task needs.

For example, one browser window for the task you're on, and close the tabs from the last one.

Every app that's open and blinking at you is an invitation to switch.

And the fifth one is to notice when you interrupt yourself.

Gloria Mark has also studied self-interruptions, which are the times we switch with nothing pinging us at all.

So when you feel the urge to check Slack, ask yourself if anything actually came in.

And if your team has no agreement on where things live, you can be the one who asks for it.

So tell me in the comments, which two apps do you switch between the most at work?

script:
### Open

Something happens in the world, and within one hour, everybody has a take.

You see it on X and TikTok, and in the family WhatsApp group.

And everyone is very, very sure.

If you're not careful, you pick up an opinion before you even know what happened.

My boyfriend always jokes that I'm an overthinker. A deep thinker.

I even have think-out-loud sessions with Claude, where I talk through my ideas.

So today, the overthinker is going through what I do to think clearly when everyone around me is already sure.

It starts with slowing down, and it ends with changing your mind without feeling ashamed.

### Slow down before you react

The first habit is slowing down before you react to anything online.

When I see a hot take, the first thing I try to do is nothing.

I don't reply, and I don't share it or quote it with my own opinion on top.

I wait.

And I wait because the things that spread fastest online are often the things that are not true.

In 2018, researchers at MIT published a study of about 126,000 news stories that were shared on Twitter between 2006 and 2017.

They found that false news was 70 percent more likely to be retweeted than true news.

*[on screen: false news was 70% more likely to be retweeted than the truth (Vosoughi, Roy and Aral, Science, 2018)]*

And the researchers found that people, more than bots, were the ones spreading it.

People like you and me, pressing share.

So why do we share things that aren't true?

Two researchers, Gordon Pennycook and David Rand, have studied this for years.

Their work suggests that a lot of the time, people share false things because they never stopped to ask if it was true. Their attention was on something else, like whether the post was funny, or whether it proved their point.

In one experiment, they sent a message to more than 5,000 Twitter users.

The message asked them to rate how accurate one headline was. That's all.

And afterwards, the news those users shared came from more reliable sources, on average.

The change was small. But one question did that.

*[on screen: "How accurate is this headline?" One question improved the quality of news people shared afterwards (Pennycook et al., Nature, 2021)]*

When a post makes me feel something strong, angry, or scared, or very proud, I try to take that as my cue to wait.

Before I ask "should I share this?", I ask "is this true?"

I read past the headline. I open the actual article.

And if you're on WhatsApp, look out for the label that says "Forwarded many times," with two arrows.

WhatsApp says that label goes on messages that have been forwarded many times.

So it probably didn't start with the person who sent it to you. It came through a long chain of people.

That's a good moment to check before you forward it again.

### How to tell a fact from an opinion

The second habit is separating the facts from the opinions, because most posts mix the two together.

A fact is something you can check. You can prove it or disprove it with evidence.

An opinion is what someone believes, or what they value.

Both are allowed. I have plenty of opinions. You've watched my videos.

The trouble starts when a fact and an opinion come in one sentence, and you swallow both at once.

And telling them apart is harder than it sounds.

In 2018, Pew Research Center tested a little over 5,000 adults in America.

They showed people ten statements from the news. Five were factual, five were opinions, and people had to say which was which.

Only 26 percent got all five factual statements right.

And only 35 percent got all five opinions right.

*[on screen: 26% correctly labelled all five factual statements, 35% all five opinions (Pew Research Center, 2018)]*

Would you get all ten? I'm not sure I would.

Pew also found that people were more likely to call a statement factual when it favoured their own political side.

That study was in America. I haven't seen the same test done in Nigeria, but I don't think we'd do very differently.

So this is how I practise it. Take a made-up post like this one.

*[on screen: "Estonia has made master's degrees free for every African student. Best country in Europe. Apply before it's too late!" (label it made-up example)]*

"Estonia has made master's degrees free for every African student."

That's a factual claim. It could be true or it could be false, but you can check it, on the university's own website.

"Best country in Europe."

That's an opinion. Someone is allowed to feel that way, but you can't check it.

"Apply before it's too late."

That one is pressure. It's there to make you move fast.

So in that whole post, the part you can check is one sentence.

And that's the sentence to go and check.

### How to check a source like a fact checker

The third habit is checking the source, and the best trick I know for this comes from professional fact checkers.

At Stanford, two researchers, Sam Wineburg and Sarah McGrew, watched three groups of people judge websites.

Ten professional fact checkers. Ten historians with PhDs. And twenty-five Stanford students.

One task was to compare two websites about children's health.

One was the American Academy of Pediatrics, a big professional body for children's doctors.

The other was the American College of Pediatricians, a much smaller group with a very similar name, which started as a protest against one of the Academy's positions.

Both websites look professional.

Every fact checker said the Academy's site was the more reliable one.

Most of the students picked the other one.

The difference was what the fact checkers did first.

On average, they left the College's page in about half a minute.

They opened new tabs, searched for the organisation itself, and read what other people said about it.

The researchers call this reading laterally. You read sideways, across tabs, instead of only going down the page.

*[on screen: fact checkers "read laterally, leaving a site after a quick scan" (Wineburg and McGrew, Stanford)]*

The historians and the students mostly stayed on the page and read it carefully, from top to bottom.

And a well-designed page can fool a careful reader.

So when you see a claim from a source you don't know, open a new tab before you read it closely, and search who is behind it.

The other half of checking a source is going back to the original.

If it's a screenshot of a headline, find the actual article.

If the article says "a study found," find the study, and at least read the summary at the top.

A lot of the time, the original says something smaller and more careful than the post that went viral.

*[on screen: link to my video on how I read research papers, if it's live]*

If research papers feel scary to read, I have a video on how I read them.

### Find the best version of the other side

The fourth habit is finding the best version of the side you disagree with.

The opposite of this is called a straw man.

A straw man is when you take the weakest, silliest version of someone's argument and knock it down, because it's easy.

A steelman goes the other way. You build the strongest version of their argument, the best case they could make, and you deal with that one.

In 1859, the philosopher John Stuart Mill wrote, "He who knows only his own side of the case, knows little of that."

*[on screen: "He who knows only his own side of the case, knows little of that." John Stuart Mill, On Liberty (1859)]*

And the philosopher Daniel Dennett, in his book Intuition Pumps, wrote down a rule I really like. He credits it to a game theorist called Anatol Rapoport.

Before you criticise someone, Dennett says, "You should attempt to re-express your target's position so clearly, vividly, and fairly that your target says, 'Thanks, I wish I'd thought of putting it that way.'"

*[on screen: the Dennett quote, with "Intuition Pumps and Other Tools for Thinking (2013)"]*

So that's my test.

Could I explain your side so well that you'd say, yes, that's exactly what I mean?

If I can't, I'm not ready to argue with you yet.

In practice, skip the angriest person on the other side, and find the calmest, smartest person who disagrees with you, and read them in their own words, instead of in a screenshot posted by someone who can't stand them.

Let me give you an example that a lot of us will recognise.

Say you're convinced that every young Nigerian should japa, and go and study abroad.

The straw man of the other side is "they're just jealous," or "they don't want you to succeed."

The steelman is someone who says the money for one year abroad could start a business at home.

And that the first years abroad can be lonely and hard, so some people would build a better life by staying.

You might still disagree with them at the end. That's fine.

But now you disagree with the real argument, and your own opinion is stronger for it.

### How to notice your own biases

The fifth habit is noticing your own biases, and I think this is the hardest one.

A bias is a shortcut your brain takes that pushes your thinking in one direction, usually without you noticing.

There are a lot of them, so I'll name five quickly, and then explain the three I think matter most for opinions.

*[on screen: list of the five as she names them]*

Confirmation bias is when you look for, and remember, the things that agree with what you already believe.

The bandwagon effect is when you believe something more because a lot of people around you believe it.

Motivated reasoning is when you reason your way to the answer you wanted from the start.

The bias blind spot is when you see bias in other people much more easily than in yourself.

And the illusion of explanatory depth is when you think you understand something better than you do.

Let's start with motivated reasoning, because there's a study that shows it really clearly.

Dan Kahan and his colleagues at Yale gave about 1,100 American adults a small table of numbers from a made-up study, and asked them what the results showed.

For some people, the table was about a cream for skin rashes.

For others, the exact same numbers were about a ban on carrying hidden guns, and whether crime went up or down.

When the topic was skin cream, people's maths skills predicted whether they got it right.

When the topic was guns, people were much more likely to get it right when the correct answer matched their politics, and to get it wrong when it didn't.

So when I find something that agrees with me perfectly, I ask myself one question.

If this same evidence pointed the other way, would I accept it this easily?

*[optional line]*

The next one is about all of us.

In 2002, Emily Pronin and her colleagues at Stanford asked people how much common biases affected them, compared with other people, like the average American or their own classmates.

People rated themselves as less biased than everybody else.

And even after the researchers explained how the bias could have affected them, people still insisted their own ratings were accurate and objective.

That's the bias blind spot.

Knowing about biases doesn't make you free of them. That includes me, making a whole video about it.

And the last one is a test you can do on yourself right now.

In 2002, Leonid Rozenblit and Frank Keil at Yale asked people how well they understood everyday things, like a zip, a flush toilet, or a lock.

People rated themselves quite high.

Then they were asked to write out, step by step, how the thing works.

And after trying, they rated their understanding lower.

So try it now. How does a zip work? Explain it, step by step.

*[on screen: How does a zip work? Explain it step by step.]*

*[pause]*

If that was harder than you expected, you're in good company.

So what I would tell you is, before you argue about how something works, try to explain it, step by step, to yourself first.

A lot of the time, you'll find you only know the headline.

### How to change your mind without shame

The last habit is changing your mind, without feeling ashamed of it.

I think a lot of us grew up feeling that being wrong is embarrassing. That if you change your position, you've lost.

And I think we overestimate how bad it looks.

In 2015, two psychologists, Adam Fetterman and Kai Sassenberg, surveyed 281 scientists, and asked them to imagine one of their findings failing when other researchers tried to repeat it.

The scientists expected that to hurt their reputation more when the finding was their own than when it was a colleague's.

But when they judged other scientists, they rated the ones who admitted they were wrong more favourably than the ones who defended themselves.

It was a survey, so it can't tell us exactly what happens in real life.

But it suggests we fear admitting we're wrong more than we need to.

And I want to show you what changing your mind well looks like, with a real example.

In 2017, William Brady and his colleagues looked at more than 500,000 tweets about topics like gun control and climate change.

They found that each extra word carrying both a moral judgment and a feeling, words like abuse or spite, made a tweet spread about 20 percent more.

That number got quoted a lot.

Then in 2025, Brady and his colleagues pooled 27 studies, with millions of posts.

The effect was still there, but smaller. Closer to 12 percent for each word.

*[on screen: 2017: about 20% more spread per moral-emotional word. 2025, 27 studies pooled: about 12% (Brady et al., PNAS and PNAS Nexus)]*

The same researcher went back, looked at more data, and published a smaller number than his famous one.

I trust that research more because of it.

So this is what I would tell you.

Before you pick a side on something, ask yourself, what would change my mind?

If you can't think of anything at all, ask yourself whether you're still thinking about it.

Practise saying out loud, "I used to think this, and now I think that."

And as an overthinker, I'll tell you this. Let yourself say, "I don't know yet."

I've said this before and I still believe it. Curiosity is the state of having an open question.

"I don't know yet" keeps the question open.

So tell me in the comments, what's something you changed your mind about recently?

And what made you change it?

script:
### Open

My brain is rotting.

Okay, I'm being a little bit dramatic. I don't think my brain is rotting per se.

But I used to read for hours, every day, back to back, and I genuinely enjoyed it.

These days, I struggle to read at the level I want to.

So I'm trying to reverse it. In this video, I'll show you what I'm doing, and what the research says actually helps.

Because if you talk to me for fifteen seconds, I'll mention this topic. It's shocking me.

### What brain rot means

"Brain rot" was Oxford's Word of the Year for 2024.

*[on screen: brain rot (n.) "the supposed deterioration of a person's mental or intellectual state, especially viewed as the result of overconsumption of material (now particularly online content) considered to be trivial or unchallenging." Oxford, 2024]*

Their definition is the supposed deterioration of a person's mental or intellectual state, from consuming too much content that's trivial or unchallenging.

Oxford says "supposed," so even the dictionary isn't claiming your brain is actually decaying.

And the phrase is much older than TikTok. Oxford traced its first recorded use to 1854, in Henry David Thoreau's book Walden.

*[on screen: "While England endeavours to cure the potato rot, will not any endeavour to cure the brain-rot, which prevails so much more widely and fatally?" Henry David Thoreau, Walden, 1854]*

He asked why England was trying to cure the potato rot, when nobody was trying to cure the brain rot. So people have been worried about this for about 170 years.

For me, brain rot is a whole cluster of things happening.

Shortened attention span. Compulsive scrolling, at different levels for different people. Difficulty with deep reading and thinking. Mental fogginess. And a diet of low quality content.

I mean, saying the brain is rotten feels like saying it's damaged. So I wouldn't go that far.

### What brain rot looks like for me

When I talk about brain rot, I'm talking about myself too.

Personally, I don't scroll as much. I don't even think I use social media as much as the average person.

But I still think that from time to time I would indulge myself in compulsive scrolling, for like minutes.

And I don't think I read as much anymore. People meet me and they're like, oh yeah, you read, you always have a book.

But if you knew me, I used to read so much. Not light stuff, I'd read serious stuff.

I remember when I was in school, I would read for hours.

I'd stay up overnight, and I would do this every day, back to back, and I genuinely enjoyed it.

I mean, I still deep read now. I'm doing a master's programme, so I don't have a choice but to read.

But I'm having difficulty deep reading at the level that I want to deep read. And I struggle with mental fog.

Maybe I should even turn these videos to myself now.

It's like my attention is being turned into some habits that I don't like. And I've been waging war against this.

I've been so aggressive against this. And I don't even think I've been aggressive enough.

### What happened to my attention span

Where I really feel brain rot is my attention span.

I used to live on Medium, reading very long articles.

If you don't know Medium, it's a site where people publish long articles and essays.

And LinkedIn attracted me five or six years ago, because people wrote long posts there, like Substack posts.

And people actually read them and engaged with them.

Now, even me, I lose interest quickly when an article is long.

I know my attention span is getting messed up.

So everything I'm doing in this video is also how I'm trying to fix my attention span.

### Can brain rot be reversed?

Before I tell you how I'm reversing brain rot, I want to answer the obvious question. Is it real, and can it be reversed?

When Oxford announced the word, Andrew Przybylski, a psychologist at the University of Oxford, told the BBC that "there's no evidence of brain rot actually being a thing."

But that doesn't mean nothing is happening.

In 2025, a big review in Psychological Bulletin combined 71 studies, with almost 100,000 people altogether.

*[on screen: 71 studies, 98,299 people. Nguyen et al., Psychological Bulletin, 2025]*

They found that people who watched more short videos, like TikTok, Reels and YouTube Shorts, tended to have poorer attention and poorer inhibitory control.

Inhibitory control is your ability to stop yourself from doing something on impulse. Like not picking up your phone when you said you wouldn't.

But most of those studies measured people once, at one point in time.

So they can show that two things go together. They can't show which one caused the other.

Think about umbrellas. People carrying umbrellas get wet more often than people who aren't carrying one.

Umbrellas don't make you wet. Rainy days cause both.

It could be that short videos weaken your attention. It could also be that people who already struggle to focus reach for short videos more. Or both. The researchers said this themselves.

*[optional line: "Stay with me for this next study, because it actually tested cause and effect."]*

So the question I care about is whether things get better when you change what you do. And there's one experiment that tested exactly that.

In 2025, researchers in Canada and the US recruited 467 people, and used an app to block all internet on their phones for two weeks.

Calls and texts still worked. Their laptops still had internet. It was only the phone.

*[on screen: Two weeks, no mobile internet. Castelo et al., PNAS Nexus, 2025]*

After two weeks without phone internet, people did better on a computer attention test, the kind where you have to stay focused for a long stretch.

The researchers compared the size of that improvement to about ten years of age-related decline in attention. People also reported better mental health and wellbeing.

And the numbers are honest. Only about one in four people kept the block on for at least ten of the fourteen days.

But the improvement still showed up when the researchers counted everyone who signed up, including the people who didn't stick to it.

So that's why I say reversing. In that experiment, attention got better in two weeks of using the phone less.

### Using my phone less

The first thing I'm doing to reverse brain rot is using my phone less, on purpose.

When I was nineteen, I used to use Instagram a lot. And I strongly felt that it was very dysfunctional for the life I wanted to live.

So I left Instagram. I didn't use the app for about six years.

I enjoyed Instagram, by the way. At the time, I couldn't even put into words why I was leaving.

These days, my rule for social media is need.

I should only open Twitter, Instagram or TikTok when I need something from there, and my need is usually to post my content. And I break it too sometimes.

I want to be able to open social media, get what I wanted to get out of it, spend five minutes or whatever, and actively own the process of closing it.

And for some months now, I have notifications, even WhatsApp notifications, which is the one I would normally keep on, turned off on my phone.

I do want social interaction. But a lot of the interaction we have isn't even deep.

It's just us responding, commenting on a status. Everything has become so surface level, even with human interaction.

### Doing one thing at a time

Another way I'm reversing brain rot is by forcing myself not to multitask.

Because I feel like constant switching fragments my working memory. It's such a problem that I have.

I'm not a brain psychologist or whatever, but I understand that working memory is the mental workspace where thinking actually happens.

Think of it like a kitchen counter. It's where the cooking actually happens, and there's only so much space on it.

So every time I switch, I'm having to clear the counter and bring everything back out. Drop it, and reload it. Every time.

By the way, task switching is something I'm so passionate about as a topic. My master's thesis is actually about switching between tools, and I made a whole video on task switching, so I'll link it.

So I feel like, just going back and forth, I'm not reaching this deep continuous state where the level of intellectual work that I want happens.

I'm doing work, of course. But there's a kind of work, actual deep intentional work, that I want to do that I'm not reaching.

I don't know how to put this into words, man.

So now, sit with one thing, finish that thing, no exit. Even at work.

I'm retraining long attention, forcing my brain to relearn that, and to resist the urge to switch.

You see that thing where you're doing something and something else drops into your mind?

Or whatever you're doing is getting to a point where it's getting harder, and you feel like you need a break, and that always makes you switch to something else?

And then you come back, and it's just another thing.

### Letting myself be bored

I'm also reversing brain rot by letting myself be bored again.

I also don't like to get bored anymore. I used to be okay getting bored, and this is something I'm actively trying to bring back.

Because I feel like now we have to fill every gap. You're waiting in a queue. You're commuting on the bus. There's a quiet moment.

It feels like you have to fill it with something. You have to bring out your phone, scroll, do this, do that.

There's this constant ingesting, and we never really get to the point of actually digesting.

And people found it hard to sit with their own thoughts even before short videos.

In 2014, psychologists at the University of Virginia and Harvard asked people to sit alone in a room for fifteen minutes, with no phone and nothing to read. Just their thoughts.

There was a button in the room that gave a mild electric shock. Earlier, these same people had said they would pay money to avoid that shock.

67% of the men and 25% of the women pressed it at least once.

*[on screen: 15 minutes alone with their thoughts. 67% of men and 25% of women pressed the shock button at least once. Wilson et al., Science, 2014]*

Some of them would rather do something unpleasant than nothing at all. And this was 2014, before TikTok.

So I'm refilling boredom. Deliberately leaving gaps unfilled.

This year I learned how to ride a bike, and I really love it when I take it out to ride.

I try to ride at least every day, or once in two days. No headphones, no music, just riding somewhere.

And in many cases, there's nothing I'm going there to do. We're just doing one freaking boring thing.

I love music, but sometimes, no music, man.

Sometimes I stop and film places I would normally just pass by without noticing.

### Learning to read deeply again

And to reverse brain rot, I'm getting my deep reading back.

If you used to read for hours and now you can't get through a chapter, you're not the only one.

Maryanne Wolf is a scientist who studies how the brain learns to read. In 2018, she wrote a book called Reader, Come Home.

In it, she describes trying to reread a novel she had loved when she was young, Magister Ludi by Hermann Hesse.

And she couldn't get into it. She wrote, "I hated the book."

She felt she had lost what she called the "cognitive patience" to read books like that.

So she kept at it, a bit every day, until she could sink into it again.

That sounds a lot like what I'm going through. So this is what I'm doing.

When I'm waiting on something, maybe I'm working and I'm waiting on a response, or I'm waiting on Claude Code, I know there'll be gaps.

Sometimes I tend to just pick up my phone, and I'm forcing myself to pick up a book instead.

Sometimes you do the mental maths of that activity in your head and you're like, oh, I'm too lazy to do this much, so you just pick up your phone, because that is easy.

But I'm picking up more low friction things. Writing. Reading. I started handwriting scriptures these days and I really love it.

### How to fix your attention span

The reason I keep at all of this is that I understand my attention is trainable.

I believe what you practise, you get better at. And I know that if I keep distracting myself, I cannot do deep work.

I'm training myself. And I hate it every time that I do it.

I know that I am freaking training myself, with this whole context switching, going back and forth.

I know that I'm training myself to become something I don't want to.

And I believe all of this is reversible. That's the part I'm working on currently.

Just altogether working on my attention, my impulse control, my mental consolidation. Just everything.

Cal Newport, a computer science professor at Georgetown who writes about focus, has a name for this kind of work.

In a New York Times essay this year, he argued for what he calls "cognitive fitness."

His comparison is physical fitness. If your body was out of shape, you'd start a routine and build up slowly. He says we can do the same for our minds.

*[on screen: "cognitive fitness." Cal Newport, The New York Times, March 2026]*

And Daniel Pink, in his video on how to fix your attention span, starts with a simple step.

Get a book and time yourself. How long can you read before you get up or check your phone?

Write that time down. That's your baseline. Then you stretch it a little at a time, like a muscle.

*[on screen: time how long you can read without getting up or checking your phone. That's your baseline. Daniel Pink, "How To Fix Your Attention Span"]*

If you feel like brain rot is happening to you too, don't panic about your brain. There's no evidence it's rotting.

Pick one thing you can actually keep, and keep it. For me, it started with one app at nineteen.

I'm sounding like an influencer. But yeah, what are we all doing about brain rot?

Tell me in the comments one thing you've really tried, even if it only worked a little. I want to hear it.

script:
### Open

Mental convenience is killing our cognitive ability.

I've been thinking about this for a while, and I don't think I have fully worked it out yet. So yeah.

I'm thinking aloud, and you can disagree with me.

I feel like so many things that used to take mental effort for us have been made so easy. And it's not even just the big things.

So many little things too. And I really think that that is shifting something.

So in this video, I'll show you what I mean, what the research says about GPS, Google and ChatGPT, and where I've landed.

### The little things we don't do anymore

So what do I mean by mental convenience? Let me lay it out in more straightforward terms.

We don't navigate roads manually anymore. We follow our GPS. We follow a voice.

I don't remember things anymore. I remember where to find things.

We don't spell as much. We don't do arithmetic. We don't even finish our own sentences, there's autocomplete.

And that autocomplete one has actually been studied, in my own field.

In 2020, Kenneth Arnold and Krzysztof Gajos at Harvard, with Krysta Chauncey, asked people to write captions for pictures, some with predictive text suggestions and some without.

With the suggestions, people wrote shorter captions, and they used fewer of the words the system wasn't predicting.

So the suggestions changed what people actually wrote.

*[on screen: with predictive text, captions were shorter and used fewer words the system didn't predict (Arnold, Chauncey & Gajos, 2020)]*

I was seeing someone talking about this thing they use that summarises books for them, and in my head I'm thinking, if you want to read, just read.

Why are you reading the summary of an amazing book? I promise you, read the book itself if you really want to read it.

And it's not even an academic book. It's fiction. Why are you reading the summary of that?

We don't even pick the things we watch. I don't even pick the things I watch, honestly.

Maybe I want to see a movie, which is not an activity I really enjoy anymore.

But I would rather just see a movie that someone talked about, that I saw someone rant about. The algorithm picks what I watch.

I don't keep phone numbers in my head anymore. I don't keep birthdays in my head anymore.

If I know you, I probably have your birthday in my calendar or something.

So I think mental effort is being consistently removed from ordinary day-to-day life. And that is accumulating.

That removal of mental effort is accumulating for us.

### I build convenience for a living

By the way, just so this video about mental convenience doesn't sound dishonest.

I build convenient things for a living. I myself love convenience. Like, I love convenience so much.

I am a software developer.

My actual job, the thing that I get paid for, is removing steps. Making things faster. Making a flow shorter.

Taking a thing that would have taken a user longer, and making it faster, shorter, easier. That is what I do.

And on top of that, my field, the field I do research in, human-computer interaction, at its core is largely about making things easier for people to use.

Reducing friction. Reducing cognitive load. Not making the user have to think too much, or stress too much.

So I'm literally existing inside the very thing that I'm speaking against.

And to be honest, I don't even think I'm speaking against it. I'm just observing.

And even for myself as a user, I am the master of looking for convenience. I use AI every time. I use Google Maps.

Anything that will make things easy for me, I will use it. I will pay for a subscription that will make my life easier.

And as a professional, I understand how deliberately mental friction is being removed for the end user.

If you get something that makes work easy for you, trust me, it's not something that just happened accidentally.

People sat down and decided to remove that friction for you. And I've been part of those people in my own professional life as well.

### What GPS does to your brain

*[optional line: "And this is the part that shook me."]*

The clearest research on mental convenience is about GPS, and how we find our way around.

And it starts with London taxi drivers.

To drive a black cab in London, drivers have to learn something called the Knowledge.

That's about 25,000 streets, and thousands of landmarks, all in their heads. It usually takes three to four years.

*[on screen: the Knowledge: about 25,000 streets, thousands of places, usually 3 to 4 years]*

A neuroscientist at University College London, Eleanor Maguire, studied their brains.

She looked at the hippocampus. That's a part of your brain that does a lot of the work for memory, and for finding your way around.

In 2011, she and Katherine Woollett followed 79 trainees through the training.

The 39 trainees who passed had more grey matter in that back part of the hippocampus by the end.

The ones who didn't pass didn't show that change.

So years of practising finding your way changed something in the brain.

Now, what happens when you hand that job to your phone?

In 2017, Hugo Spiers and his team at UCL scanned 24 people while they found their way around a simulation of Soho, in London.

When people chose their own route, their hippocampus got more active every time they entered a new street.

When they followed directions, those areas didn't respond to the street network in the same way.

Hugo Spiers put it like this: "In that sense our brain has switched off its interest in the streets around us."

Then in 2020, Louisa Dahmani and Véronique Bohbot at McGill University in Canada tested 50 regular drivers.

The people who had used GPS more in their lives had worse spatial memory when they had to find their way without it, in virtual navigation tests.

About three years later, they retested 13 of those people. The ones who had used GPS more in those three years had a steeper decline.

And before you say maybe people who are bad with directions just use GPS more, they checked that.

The heavy GPS users didn't report a worse sense of direction. So it looks like the GPS use came first.

But that follow-up was only 13 people, and the researchers themselves say it needs a bigger study.

So I take it as a strong hint, and I'd love to see the bigger study.

### The Google effect

And mental convenience is not even an AI thing. People have been talking about this for over a decade.

Our brains are becoming pretty economical.

For example, my brain will probably not want to put in the effort to remember something that I can access somewhere again.

There's a study from 2011, in the journal Science, by Betsy Sparrow, Jenny Liu and Daniel Wegner. People call it the Google effect.

What they found is that when people expected to have access to information later, they remembered the information itself less, and they remembered where to find it more.

*[on screen: expect to look it up later, and you remember WHERE it is more than WHAT it is (Sparrow, Liu & Wegner, 2011)]*

But I have to be careful with this one, because when other scientists tried to repeat it, it didn't hold up so well.

A big replication project in 2018 couldn't repeat the first experiment, and neither could a team in Germany in 2020.

And a team in 2021 found the "I'll forget what I saved" effect only when people first saw that the computer really would save their work.

So I hold this one loosely. I think my brain does make that trade sometimes. How strong the effect is, scientists are still arguing about.

### Offloading isn't the problem

Handing mental work to something outside your head, like putting a meeting in your calendar, is what psychologists call cognitive offloading.

But then again, I'm not saying that offloading mental work to tools is bad.

Writing itself, writing, that we think so highly of, is pretty much offloading.

It's offloading something from your brain, and it's been such a good idea for thousands of years.

And funny enough, even writing had people worried.

In Plato's Phaedrus, which is about 2,400 years old, Socrates tells a story where an Egyptian king says writing "will create forgetfulness in the learners' souls, because they will not use their memories."

I'm very glad people kept writing anyway.

So I don't think offloading is even the problem here. I'm talking through my thoughts here.

There's a whole philosophical position that your tools become part of your thinking rather than a replacement for it. The philosophers Andy Clark and David Chalmers called it the extended mind.

And there's this concept in HCI that I learned about, oh my goodness, distributed cognition. Yeah, distributed cognition.

It comes a lot from Edwin Hutchins, who studied how the crew of a navy ship navigated together, with their charts and their instruments.

And basically the whole idea is that your cognition is not limited to your mind. The tools you use are part of your thinking.

They're not a replacement for it.

So it cannot be that offloading is the problem. I feel like something else is going on. Or maybe I'm overthinking.

Like, I am such an evil overthinker.

### What we offload matters

So I don't think offloading is the problem with mental convenience, but I also think something else is going on somewhere.

There's some mental convenience that is resulting in a reduction in cognitive ability for us.

And when I was thinking about it, and this is not even finished, I'm still thinking, I'm thinking perhaps it is what we are offloading that is the problem.

Maybe it's because we are offloading the result, or we are offloading our thinking process. And we build the ability by thinking.

So if I read the summary of a book, that gives me information. But it wouldn't do to me what reading the book will actually do to me.

And also, there's this state where you don't know what you're thinking yet.

Have you ever followed through your thinking process, and there's this part, this time, where you haven't really gotten your thoughts yet, but you're approaching it?

I don't know if I'm the only one this happens to.

You can feel yourself approaching your thoughts, but you haven't gotten there quite yet.

I feel like that part is where something is. That part is where we are either missing it, or we are shortening it.

### What happened when ChatGPT wrote the essays

There's one AI study that fits this idea of offloading the thinking, and I want to tell you about it carefully.

It's from the MIT Media Lab, led by Nataliya Kosmyna, and it's called "Your Brain on ChatGPT."

They had 54 people write essays over four months.

One group used ChatGPT. One group used a search engine. And one group used only their brains.

They wore EEG caps while they wrote, which pick up electrical activity in the brain.

The researchers wrote that brain connectivity "systematically scaled down with the amount of external support."

So the brain-only group showed the strongest connections, the search engine group was in the middle, and the ChatGPT group was the weakest.

And the ChatGPT group had trouble quoting from the essays they had written just minutes before. They also didn't feel much ownership of their essays.

*[on screen: brain only > search engine > ChatGPT (brain connectivity, EEG). Preprint, 54 people, 18 in the final session.]*

Now, I really want to be careful here.

This is a preprint, which means when it came out in June 2025, it hadn't been peer reviewed.

It's small. 54 people, and only 18 of them came back for the last session.

And it's one task, writing essays, in a lab.

The lead author herself told Scientific American that the study showed "no dumbness in the brain, no stupidity, no brain on vacation."

So please don't share it as "ChatGPT makes you dumb." The study doesn't say that.

What it does fit, for me, is the difference between offloading the result and offloading the thinking.

I think struggling to quote your own essay is what you'd expect if the thinking part got skipped.

I made a separate video on how I use AI as a master's student without letting it think for me, so I won't go into my own setup here.

### Convenience feels productive

I think I've said this in another video before, that attention is trainable.

But I don't even think it's just attention that is trainable. I think thinking is trainable.

So every convenient route that doesn't require me to use my mind as much is a training that I'm not doing.

And convenience feels good. It feels productive. It feels like being smart with your time.

I mean, if you finish something faster than you expected, you don't sit down and start thinking, oh, what part of this did I skip?

What made me get to the end of it so fast? You just count it as a win, right?

And I think that's what makes it slippery.

Sometimes now I'll do something and it feels like it took me so little time, and in my head it feels like, you know when you have too much money and you're like, what bill did I not pay?

Why do I have so much money? What bill did I forget to pay?

Yeah. That feeling.

### Where I've landed on mental convenience

So I think there is so much mental convenience.

And I would rather be inconvenient in the few places where the ability is one that I want to keep.

Because there are some abilities that I would love to keep, and it's not just about the results that they give me.

I want to retain the abilities themselves. And I'm actually starting to be more intentional about those parts.

For me, reading is one of them. I read almost every day, and there is always a book in my bag.

If you want to try this too, this is what I would tell you.

Pick the few abilities you actually want to keep. If you don't care about doing maths in your head, let the calculator have it.

For the ones you care about, try first, before you reach for the tool. If it's finding your way, look at the map before you leave, and only check it again when you're stuck.

If you want to read a book, read the book.

And when you use AI for something that matters to you, write your own rough version first, even if it's messy. That messy part is where your thinking happens.

I like things that work. I love using things to make work easy for myself.

I just want to know that there's a cost to the mental convenience I reach out for.

And I'm so convinced that that cost comes in cognitive ability, that there's a loss of ability somewhere.

Anyway, tell me if you think I'm wrong, because I'm still turning this one over.

And tell me if there's something you used to be able to do that you've noticed you can't do as easily now.

### Open

I use AI every day, at work as a developer and in my master's here in Tallinn.

Mostly Claude.

And I have one rule for myself.

AI can help me think, but it doesn't get to do the thinking for me.

So in this video, I'll show you the five ways I use AI as a master's student, the things I don't let it touch, and what my university's rules say.

But first, I want to show you why I'm this careful, because there's a study that explains it better than I can.

### Why I don't let AI do my thinking

Why would a student who uses AI every day be careful with it?

For me, it's about what happens when the AI goes away.

In 2025, a group of researchers published a study in PNAS, which is one of the big science journals.

They worked with nearly a thousand high school maths students in Turkey.

Some students got a normal ChatGPT-style assistant while they practised.

Some got a version that was designed to give hints instead of answers.

And some got no AI at all.

While they had the AI, the students with the normal version did 48% better on the practice problems than the students with nothing.

The hint version did 127% better.

Then the AI was taken away, and everyone sat an exam.

The students who had practised with the normal version did 17% worse than the students who never had AI at all.

The students with the hint version did about the same as the students with no AI.

*[on screen: Bastani et al., PNAS 2025. Practice with normal AI: +48%. Exam without it: -17%. Hint version: +127% in practice, about the same in the exam]*

So think about it like a friend who does your homework for you every week.

Your homework looks great.

Then exam day comes, and your friend isn't allowed in the exam hall.

That's what I worry about.

It can feel like you're learning when you're mostly watching.

And the hint version tells us something useful too, because it shows that how you use the AI changes what you get from it.

So everything I'm about to show you is me trying to be the hint version for myself.

### What my university says about using AI

Before you use AI for anything in your studies, check what your school says about it, because the rules are different everywhere.

At my university, Tallinn University, there's a page of recommendations on using AI.

It says students can use AI as a study partner, for generating ideas, for self-check, for correcting texts and translating, for making summaries while you learn, and as a programming aid.

It also says the teaching staff can decide how much AI you can use in their course.

And this is the line I want you to hear.

Using AI where your teacher has limited it, or not properly referencing your use of AI, is considered academic fraud.

The same page says the author is fully responsible for the content of the work, even when AI helped make it.

*[on screen: Tallinn University: "failure to make proper reference to the use of AI is considered academic fraud." The author "is fully responsible for the content and form of the presented work."]*

The university even gives us access to some AI tools, like ChatGPT Edu and Google Gemini.

So my school is fine with AI, as long as you're open about how you used it and you own what you hand in.

That's my school, as of October 2026.

TalTech, another university in the same city, has its own separate AI regulation from July 2026.

So even two universities in one city don't share one rulebook.

Please read your own school's AI rules, its plagiarism rules, and your course outline, before you open an AI tool for an assignment.

And if anything isn't clear, ask your lecturer in the first week, not the night before the deadline.

### Habit 1, I make AI quiz me

The first way I use AI as a student is to make it quiz me.

Most of us study by reading our notes again and again.

It feels like learning, because the words start to look familiar.

But what you need on exam day is to remember it when the page is closed.

There's an old study on this from 2006, by Henry Roediger and Jeffrey Karpicke at Washington University in St. Louis.

Students read a short passage.

One group kept reading it again and again.

Another group read it once, and then kept testing themselves by writing down what they could remember.

A week later, the testing group remembered 61% of the passage.

The re-reading group remembered 40%.

And the re-reading group had read the passage about 14 times, while the testing group read it about 3 times.

The re-reading group also felt more sure that they knew it.

*[on screen: Roediger and Karpicke, 2006. One week later: tested themselves 61%, re-read 40%]*

So AI is a quiz partner that never gets tired of you.

This is the kind of prompt I'd use.

*[on screen: code]*

```
I'm studying [topic]. Quiz me on it.
Ask me one question at a time, and wait for my answer.
Don't tell me the answer until I've tried.
At the end, tell me which ones I got wrong and why.
```

The "one question at a time" part matters.

If it lists ten questions with the answers under them, your eyes will read the answers.

If your course allows it, you can paste in your own notes, so the questions match what your lecturer actually covered.

What I would tell you is to close your notes before the quiz starts.

### Habit 2, I ask AI to argue against my idea

The second way I use AI as a student is to make it argue against my idea.

AI tools can lean towards agreeing with you.

In April 2025, OpenAI rolled back an update to ChatGPT after people shared screenshots of it praising questionable ideas.

OpenAI said that version had become "overly supportive but disingenuous."

So if you ask "is my idea good?", there's a good chance you'll hear yes.

And when your lecturer reads it, they might not be that kind.

So I ask the opposite question.

*[on screen: code]*

```
Here is my argument: [your argument].
Argue against it as strongly as you can.
Give me the three strongest objections a lecturer would raise.
Don't soften them.
```

Then the thinking part is mine.

I don't accept its objections just because they sound smart, either.

I go through them one by one, and I decide which ones are real, and I answer those in my own words.

Some of them will be weak.

Some will make you change your argument.

Either way, you've thought about your idea harder than you did before you asked.

Tallinn University's page lists something close to this as a good use, which is using AI for developing critical thinking, for example by analysing the answers it gives you.

### Habit 3, I try first, then ask AI to explain

The third way I use AI as a student is to explain a concept, but only after I've tried to explain it myself.

This is an example from my field.

Say I'm trying to understand cognitive load, which is roughly how much your brain is juggling at one time.

Before I ask anything, I write two or three sentences of what I think it means.

Then I paste my sentences in and ask this.

*[on screen: code]*

```
This is my understanding of [concept]: [your sentences].
What's wrong or missing?
Don't rewrite it for me. Just point to the gaps.
```

When you try first, you find the exact spot where you're stuck.

So when the explanation comes, it lands on that spot.

If you ask first, you read a perfect paragraph, you nod, and it feels like you understood it.

Then someone asks you about it in class, and the words are gone.

This is close to the hint version in the maths study.

The students who got hints instead of answers did much better in practice, and they didn't lose out in the exam.

You can ask for that directly.

Tell it, "Don't give me the answer. Give me a hint."

### Habit 4, AI never writes what I'm graded on

The fourth habit is the strictest one, and that's that AI never writes anything I'll be graded on.

That's my own rule, and it's stricter than my school's page, which allows things like correcting texts.

I have two reasons.

The first one is that an assignment is how your lecturer sees your thinking.

If AI writes it, they're grading the AI's thinking, and you're still the one responsible for every word.

Remember, at my school, not referencing your AI use is academic fraud, and the author is fully responsible for the work.

The second reason is that, for a lot of people, writing is where you find out if your idea holds together.

You think you understand something, then you try to write the paragraph, and you can't.

That moment is useful, because it shows you what you still need to learn.

If AI writes the paragraph, you skip that moment.

*[optional line]*

And the last habit is the one that can save you from embarrassing yourself in front of your lecturer.

So around graded work, AI can quiz me before, argue with my idea, and explain the concept I got stuck on.

But the words I submit are mine.

If you use AI anywhere your course allows, reference it the way your course asks you to.

### Habit 5, I check every source AI gives me

The fifth way I use AI as a student is with a rule, and it's that I check every source it gives me.

AI tools can make up citations that look completely real.

They come with authors' names, a journal and a year, and they look like any other reference.

In 2023, William Walters and Esther Isabelle Wilder published a study in Scientific Reports.

They used ChatGPT to write 84 short papers, which came with 636 citations.

With GPT-3.5, 55% of the citations were made up.

With GPT-4, it was 18%.

And many of the real ones had mistakes in them.

*[on screen: Walters and Wilder, Scientific Reports 2023. Made-up citations: GPT-3.5 55%, GPT-4 18%]*

Those were the versions of ChatGPT from that time, and the tools have changed since.

But this still happens, even to big companies.

In October 2025, the Associated Press reported that Deloitte would partially refund the Australian government for a report that cost 440,000 Australian dollars.

The report had apparent AI-generated errors, including references to research papers that don't exist, and a made-up quote from a court judgment.

Tallinn University's page says it plainly too.

It says this kind of technology "does not know" which answers are right or wrong.

So this is how I check.

I copy the title of the paper and search for it in Google Scholar or my library's database.

If it exists, I open it, and I find the part that's supposed to say what the AI said it says.

Because a real paper can still be cited for something it never said.

Think of it like a classmate who tells you "I read it somewhere."

You'd still want to see where.

### What I would tell you about using AI as a student

If you're a student and you use AI, this is what I would tell you.

Read your school's AI rules and its plagiarism rules first, and ask your lecturer if anything isn't clear.

Make AI quiz you, instead of reading your notes for the tenth time.

When you have an idea, ask it to argue against you, and then decide for yourself which objections are real.

When you don't understand something, try to explain it first, and ask it for the gaps.

Don't let it write the thing you'll be graded on.

And check every source it gives you with your own eyes.

I think AI is one of the most useful tools I have as a student.

And I want to finish this master's able to think without it too.

So tell me in the comments, what's one way you use AI for school or work that makes you think more?

script:
### Open

In June this year, the Federal Executive Council approved a big set of changes to NYSC.

To me, that's the government agreeing that the old way wasn't working.

But I don't think the changes go far enough.

I think NYSC has outlived its purpose.

It either needs to go, or be replaced with something actually productive, for the young people in it and for the country.

Right now, it's just a redundant inconvenience.

### Why NYSC was created in 1973

NYSC, the National Youth Service Corps, was created in May 1973, under General Yakubu Gowon, about three years after the civil war.

*[on screen: NYSC, created 22 May 1973, Decree No. 24, General Yakubu Gowon]*

The idea was to post young graduates far from where they grew up, so a generation that had lived with each other would find it harder to see each other as enemies.

For 1973, I think that made a lot of sense.

### Why you can't just skip NYSC

If you're not Nigerian, you might be wondering why graduates don't just skip NYSC.

The reason is the certificate.

The NYSC Act says it's the duty of every prospective employer to demand your NYSC certificate, or your exemption certificate, before they employ you.

*[on screen: NYSC Act, section 12: "it shall be the duty of every prospective employer to demand and obtain from any person" a copy of the Certificate of National Service, or an exemption certificate]*

So if you're meant to serve and you don't, a lot of doors close, especially government jobs.

### The safety problem with NYSC

The part of NYSC that makes me angry is safety.

After the 2011 elections, Human Rights Watch reported that, quote, "rioters killed ten youth corps members" in Bauchi State.

*[on screen: Human Rights Watch, May 2011: "In total, rioters killed ten youth corps members in the state." (Bauchi State)]*

In August 2023, eleven prospective corps members were kidnapped in Zamfara State on their way to camp, and some were still being held months later.

*[on screen: August 2023, 11 prospective corps members kidnapped in Zamfara on their way to camp. Some were still held in February 2024 (NYSC, via The ICIR)]*

So the state compels you to serve.

And then the state can't guarantee your safety while you serve.

Nobody should have to risk their life to get the certificate they need for a job.

### What the NYSC year actually gives you

Even when NYSC is safe, there's still the question of what the year actually gives you.

A lot of corps members are posted to work that has nothing to do with what they studied. You studied engineering, and you end up teaching in a secondary school.

The allowance is 77,000 naira a month. In my opinion, that's still small for a full year of a graduate's life.

*[on screen: NYSC monthly allowance: ₦33,000 (from 2020), ₦77,000 (paid from March 2025)]*

So for a lot of graduates, NYSC is a pause button on a life they're trying to start.

### The case for keeping NYSC, and my answer

Now, there are real arguments for keeping NYSC.

For a lot of people, it's the first time they live outside their region, and some meet their husband or wife during service.

In many rural communities, corps members are the teachers and the health workers.

And for some graduates, the place they serve becomes their first job.

Those are real. But I don't think any of them needs the year to be compulsory.

On unity, we're all on the same internet now. We're in each other's comments and in each other's DMs.

If a village school only has a teacher because a corps member was posted there for one year, I think that's a staffing problem. Those communities deserve teachers who are paid properly and who stay.

### The 2026 reform, and what I would do instead

So what about the 2026 NYSC reform?

It was approved on the 29th of June. It brings a six-week camp, eleven career streams, and postings that are meant to match your qualifications.

*[on screen: approved 29 June 2026, six-week camp, 11 career streams, skills-based postings, risk-sensitive deployment, graduation ceremony replaces the passing-out parade]*

But it's approved, and that's different from being in effect. The NYSC Act still has to be amended, and in August, the camps were still running for three weeks.

Matching people to their field is a good change. Credit where it's due.

But the year is still compulsory, whether it's useful to you or not, and whether it's safe or not.

So if it were up to me, I'd either scrap the compulsory version and let it retire with dignity, or, and this is the one I prefer, make it opt-in.

A service year you choose, that pays you enough to live on, and places you in your actual field, somewhere safe.

I think people would line up for that.

So tell me in the comments, and be honest. Was your service year worth it?
