script:
### Open

I was 18, 19 when I decided that I was going to delete Instagram from my phone.

And I did delete Instagram, and I stopped using it for six good years.

I didn't use it at all for six good years.

And I enjoyed using Instagram.

So why would a 19-year-old girl delete an app she enjoys?

In this video, I'm going to try to put that into words, with some research that helped me understand it.

And I'll give you one question you can ask yourself, that shows you how much of your life social media is deciding for you.

### Why I deleted Instagram at 19

I've always had a very strong opinion about social media.

When I deleted Instagram at 19, I don't know what it was at the time.

I was so young. I didn't know how to put it in words.

I remember I used to use Instagram a lot.

And I feel like if I had continued using Instagram at that rate, I probably would have turned out to be one big influencer or something.

But there was just something so strong in me about Instagram.

One of the things I say, even though it sounds so serious when I say it, is that it felt like this thing was going to hinder me from actually living the life that I wanted to live.

And this was at a point when it wasn't even as popular as it is now.

I already felt like, nah, this thing is doing things to me that I don't like.

As I grow older, I'm now learning to put that decision into words, because I think over it again and again.

And now I'm starting to understand why a 19-year-old girl would delete Instagram when she enjoys using it.

So I've always thought about social media as a topic very, very deeply.

I used to really write on Medium, and my most viral article on Medium is still the one I wrote about leaving Instagram for six years.

*[on screen: your Medium article about leaving Instagram]*

I think social media does a lot of things that people do not pay attention to.

And the biggest one, for me, is that it can start deciding what you do with your life.

### If you couldn't post about it, would you still do it?

There's one question I want you to ask yourself about social media.

I was telling my friend about it the other day.

I saw someone on Twitter ask it.

If you want to do anything, just about anything you're doing in your life, ask yourself, if I cannot post about this thing, will I still do it?

*[on screen: "If I couldn't post about this, would I still do it?"]*

You will realise how much stuff you're doing in your life right now that you're doing just because you can post it.

If the ability to post about that thing is removed, you probably wouldn't be doing it.

Try it with a few things from your own week.

Think about the last restaurant you picked. Would you have picked that same place if you couldn't take a single picture there?

Think about the last trip you planned. Would you still go to the same places if nobody would ever see the pictures?

Some of your answers will be yes, and that's good. Those things are yours.

But some of them will be no.

And that should make you realise that social media is actually, if you're not careful, literally dictating the way you live your life.

### What happens when you do things to post them

So what actually happens when you do something because you want to post it?

There's research on this.

In 2018, three researchers, Alixandra Barasch, Gal Zauberman and Kristin Diehl, published five studies about taking photos during experiences.

Some of them were done at real tourist sites, and some were done in a lab.

They compared people taking photos to keep for themselves with people taking photos because they wanted to share them.

The people taking photos to share enjoyed the experience less.

*[on screen: Taking photos to share lowered enjoyment. Barasch, Zauberman and Diehl, Journal of Consumer Research, 2018]*

The researchers think it's because of something called self-presentational concern.

In simple words, the moment you plan to share, part of your mind is on how you'll come across to other people.

And that worry takes some of your attention away from the thing you're actually doing.

The effect was weaker for people who care less about what others think of them, and when the photos were going to people they're close to.

A sociologist called Nathan Jurgenson wrote about this feeling back in 2011.

He called it documentary vision, and he described it as "the habit of experiencing more and more of life with the awareness of its document-potential."

*[on screen: "the habit of experiencing more and more of life with the awareness of its document-potential." Nathan Jurgenson, 2011]*

Document-potential just means, how will this look as a post?

You're at a birthday dinner, and part of you is already looking for the angle.

You're watching the sunset, and part of you is already thinking about the caption.

### Living your life on a stage

Social media can also turn more of your life into a stage.

In 1959, a sociologist called Erving Goffman wrote a book called The Presentation of Self in Everyday Life.

He described everyday life a bit like a theatre.

There's a front stage, where you know people are watching, so you perform.

And there's a back stage, where nobody is watching, and you can relax and be yourself.

Think of a waiter in a restaurant.

In the dining room, they smile and speak politely to the customers.

Then they push through the kitchen door, and they can complain about the rude customer at table four with the other staff.

Goffman was writing long before social media.

But think about what happens when your phone is always with you, and anything can become a post.

More and more of your life starts to feel like front stage.

Your holiday becomes front stage, and so can your dinner and your workout.

And when you're performing so much of the time, it gets harder to tell what you actually like, and what you're doing because it looks good.

I think that's a big part of how social media hijacks the life you want to live.

### Comparing your life to everyone else's

Another way social media shapes your life is comparison.

In 1954, a psychologist called Leon Festinger described what he called social comparison.

The idea is that we work out how we're doing by comparing ourselves with other people.

People have always done it. But social media gives you thousands of people to compare yourself with every day, and what you're seeing is their front stage.

In 2014, Erin Vogel and her colleagues found that people who used Facebook more often had lower self-esteem.

And part of that link was upward comparison, which means comparing yourself with people who seem to be doing better than you.

Instagram's own researchers found something similar.

In 2021, the Wall Street Journal reported on Instagram's internal research.

One slide said, "Social comparison is worse on Instagram."

Another said, "Thirty-two percent of teen girls said that when they felt bad about their bodies, Instagram made them feel worse."

*[on screen: Instagram internal research, reported by the Wall Street Journal, September 2021]*

Facebook pushed back, and said the slides used shorthand and didn't explain every caveat.

But think about what comparison does to your life path, over years.

You start to measure your job against the jobs that look impressive online.

You start to feel late because of where people your age seem to be.

And slowly, other people's front stage starts setting the standard for your own life.

### Mass drift

There's a creator called Ruth Guest who made a video called "How social media quickly hijacks your life path."

She uses a phrase I really like, mass drift.

In her description, she writes that many people have "fallen into the mass drift and are not living to their true selves."

She's clear that this is her own speculation, and not science.

But this person's video, it does hijack the life you want to live, if you're not careful.

Drift is slow.

You don't decide one day that you're going to live your life for an audience.

It happens one small choice at a time.

You pick this one because it'll look good. You skip that one because nobody would care to see it.

And after some years, you're living a life you didn't really choose.

And when a lot of people are seeing the same things on the same apps, a lot of people drift in the same direction. That's the mass part.

I can't prove that with a study. It's an idea.

But I think it's an idea worth checking against your own life.

### What happens when people step away from social media

So what happens when people actually step away from social media? Researchers have tested this.

In 2018, the economists Hunt Allcott, Matthew Gentzkow and their colleagues paid a randomly chosen group of American Facebook users to deactivate their accounts for four weeks, before the US midterm elections.

It freed up about an hour a day for the average person.

And they spent more of that time offline.

That included more time with friends and family, and, to be fair, more time watching TV alone.

They reported a small improvement in their wellbeing. Small, but statistically significant.

*[optional line: "And the part I find most interesting is what happened after."]*

When the four weeks were over and nobody was paying them anymore, the people who had deactivated kept using Facebook a lot less.

One participant wrote, "I've been reading books and playing the piano, which I used to do daily until the phone took over."

*[on screen: that quote. Allcott, Braghieri, Eichmeyer and Gentzkow, American Economic Review, 2020]*

Then, in 2020, a much bigger experiment, again with Allcott and Gentzkow, this time working with researchers at Meta, looked at Instagram too.

About fifteen thousand Instagram users were paid to deactivate. Some stayed off for six weeks, and the comparison group stayed off for just one week.

The people who stayed off Instagram for six weeks reported a small improvement in their emotional state.

And when the researchers looked closer, most of that came from young women, aged 18 to 24.

I couldn't help noticing that's the group I was in when I deleted Instagram.

That closer look was exploratory, and as of October 2026, the paper is a working paper, which means it hasn't been through peer review yet.

So these studies don't say leaving Instagram will change your life. The effects were small.

They do show that once people in the Facebook study stepped away, a lot of them didn't rush back.

### The other side of the social media argument

Now, I want to be fair to social media, because the other side has a real argument.

In 2019, Amy Orben and Andrew Przybylski at the University of Oxford looked at data from over 300,000 teenagers and parents.

They found that technology use explained at most 0.4% of the differences in teenagers' wellbeing.

Their comparison was that regularly eating potatoes had a similar link with wellbeing.

*[on screen: at most 0.4%. Orben and Przybylski, Nature Human Behaviour, 2019]*

Other researchers disagree with them, and that argument is still going on.

And social media gives people a lot. People find community there, they find work there, and they learn things they'd never have come across otherwise.

I post my content on these apps myself, and I want people to watch it.

This sounds a little bit hypocritical, I know.

Deleting Instagram was right for me at 19, and it doesn't have to be right for you.

I'd just like you to be the one deciding.

### My need rule and the question to ask yourself

These days I'm back on social media, because I post my content there.

And my rule for social media now is need.

I only open Instagram, or Twitter, or TikTok, when I need something from there, and my need is usually to post my content.

And I break that rule too, sometimes.

If you want to try something, this is what I would tell you.

Before you do something, ask yourself the question. If I couldn't post about this, would I still do it?

If the answer is yes, do it, and post it if you want. It's yours.

If the answer is no, you don't have to stop. But at least you'll know who you're doing it for.

And if you have that strong feeling I had at 19, that an app is getting in the way of the life you want to live, listen to it.

You can always come back. I did, six years later.

But it will do nobody any good if we are all stuck on this thing.

So tell me in the comments, what's one thing you're doing right now that you wouldn't do if you couldn't post it?

So I'm going to show you the one idea behind every regex, then build it up piece by piece, until you can read this line like a sentence. ### What a regular expression is *[on screen: a line of text, "concatenate the cat", sits in the middle of the screen. A small see-through box with the letters "cat" in it starts at the very first letter and slides one character to the right at a time. At each stop, the letters under the box flash red when they don't match and green when all three match. It turns green at "con-CAT-enate" and again at "the CAT". Both green spots stay highlighted at the end.]* A regular expression is a pattern that describes some text you're looking for. The computer takes your pattern and slides it along your text, one position at a time, asking the same question at every position. Does the text starting here match my pattern? Say your pattern is just the word cat, and your text is, "concatenate the cat." The computer starts at the first letter. Is this c-a-t? No, it's c-o-n. So it moves one step to the right and checks again. Inside "concatenate", it finds c-a-t. That's a match. Then it keeps sliding, and it finds the cat at the end too. *[on screen: regex101, pattern `cat`, test string `concatenate the cat`, both matches highlighted]* Everything else in regex is a way of making that pattern smarter. Instead of "the letters c-a-t", you can say "any digit", or "only at the start of the line". So let's make the pattern smarter, one piece at a time. ### Literals and special characters in regex *[on screen: the pattern "3.5" slides along the text "3.5 and 3x5". It lights up green on "3.5", then also lights up green on "3x5", and the "x" pulses yellow to show the dot matched it. Then a backslash drops in front of the dot ("3\.5") with a small thud, the pattern slides again, and only "3.5" lights up.]* In regex, most characters are literals. That means they match themselves. But a few characters have special jobs. *[on screen: the special characters . ^ $ * + ? ( ) []* { } | \ ] These are the ones that make regex look like rubbish. The first one is the dot. A dot means any single character, except a new line. So the pattern 3.5 matches 3.5, but it also matches 3x5, because the dot accepts any character in that spot. *[on screen: regex101, pattern `3.5`, test string `3.5 and 3x5`]* If you want a real full stop, you put a backslash in front of it. The backslash makes a special character normal again. This is called escaping. So backslash dot means an actual dot, and now only 3.5 matches. *[on screen: code]* ``` 3.5 matches 3.5 3x5 3-5 3\.5 matches 3.5 ``` The same goes for a real question mark or a real bracket. You escape it with a backslash. ### Character classes in regex *[on screen: a row of square brackets opens like a little gate, "[aeiou]* ". The text "regular expression" sits underneath. The gate slides along the text one letter at a time, and every vowel it passes over drops through the gate and lights up green, while consonants bounce off. Then the gate changes to "[0-9]" and slides over "Order 1042: 2 copies", and only the digits drop through.] A character class in regex means, match any one of these characters, and you write it with square brackets. So a, e, i, o, u inside square brackets matches any one vowel. *[on screen: regex101, pattern `[aeiou]* `, test string `regular expression`] You can also use a range with a dash. 0 to 9 in square brackets means any one digit, and small a to small z means any lowercase letter. If you put a little hat, the caret, right after the opening bracket, it flips the meaning. So caret 0 to 9 means any one character that is not a digit. *[on screen: code]* ``` [aeiou] any one vowel [0-9] any one digit [A-Za-z] any one letter [^0-9] any one character that is NOT a digit ``` Some classes are used so often that they have shortcuts. Backslash d means any digit. Backslash w means any "word character", which is a letter, a digit or an underscore. Backslash s means any whitespace, like a space, a tab or a new line. The capital versions mean the opposite. So capital D is anything that isn't a digit. *[on screen: code]* ``` \d a digit \D not a digit \w a letter, digit or _ \W not a word character \s a space, tab, newline \S not whitespace ``` On a bookstore order note, "Order 1042: 2 copies, 15000 naira", backslash d lights up every digit. *[on screen: regex101, pattern `\d`, test string `Order 1042: 2 copies, 15000 naira`]* But one at a time. To get the whole number, you need a quantifier. ### Quantifiers in regex *[on screen: the pattern "\d" sits over "Order 1042". A small "+" flies in and attaches to it. The highlight on "1" stretches like a rubber band over "0", "4", "2", and stops at the space, so "1042" is one green block. Then a side panel shows the quantifier list, and each one gets a tiny demo: "colou?r" sliding over "color colour", with the "u" fading in and out.]* A quantifier in regex says how many times the thing right before it can repeat. There are four you'll use all the time. The plus sign means one or more. So backslash d plus means one or more digits in a row. Now 1042 comes out as one match, and so does 15000. *[on screen: regex101, pattern `\d+`, test string `Order 1042: 2 copies, 15000 naira`, matches 1042, 2 and 15000]* The star means zero or more, so the thing is allowed to not be there at all. The question mark means zero or one. In other words, optional. So colou, question mark, r matches both color and colour. And curly braces give an exact number. Backslash d with 4 in curly braces means exactly four digits, and 2 comma 4 means between two and four. *[on screen: code]* ``` + one or more \d+ 1042 * zero or more \d* 1042, or nothing ? zero or one colou?r color, colour {4} exactly 4 \d{4} 2026 {2,4} between 2 and 4 \d{2,4} 42, 104, 1042 ``` The one thing to remember with quantifiers is that they only apply to the thing right before them. So in colou, question mark, r, only the u is optional. *[optional line: And if you've ever copied a validation regex from the internet, the next part might explain why it let bad data through.]* ### Anchors and word boundaries in regex *[on screen: the pattern "\d{11}" slides along "my number is 08000000000123 ok". It lights up green on the first eleven digits, even though the number is longer. A red warning flashes. Then a "^" pins itself to the left edge of the text box and a "$" pins itself to the right edge, like two nails, and the pattern now refuses to match. Second part: "\bcat\b" slides over "concatenate the cat", and two thin vertical lines appear at the edges of the word "cat" at the end, while the "cat" inside "concatenate" stays grey.]* Anchors in regex don't match any characters. They match a position. The caret, outside square brackets, means the start of the text. The dollar sign means the end. This matters for validation. Say you want to check that a phone number is exactly eleven digits, and you write backslash d, 11 in curly braces. That pattern slides along the text looking for eleven digits in a row anywhere. So a fourteen-digit number with words around it still matches. *[on screen: regex101, pattern `\d{11}`, test string `my number is 08000000000123 ok`]* Add a caret at the start and a dollar at the end. Now the whole input has to be eleven digits and nothing else. *[on screen: code]* ``` \d{11} finds 11 digits anywhere in the text ^\d{11}$ the WHOLE text must be exactly 11 digits ``` So if you're validating something, you almost always want the caret and the dollar. One more anchor is backslash b. It means a word boundary, the point where a word starts or ends. Without it, the pattern cat also matches the cat inside "concatenate". With backslash b on both sides, it only matches cat as a whole word. *[on screen: regex101, pattern `\bcat\b`, test string `concatenate the cat`, only the last "cat" matches]* ### Groups and alternation in regex *[on screen: round brackets wrap around "ha", and the pair "(ha)" turns into one solid tile. A "+" attaches to the tile, and the tile repeats across "hahaha", stamping three times. Then a "|" appears as a fork in a road: "Mr" goes up one branch, "Mrs" up another, "Ms" up the third, all merging back into one road, and the text "Mrs Obi and Mr. Bello and Ms Ade" lights up at each title.]* Groups in regex let you treat several characters as one unit. You make a group with round brackets. A quantifier only applies to the thing right before it. So ha plus means h, then one or more a's. Haaaa. But if you put ha inside brackets and then the plus, the plus applies to the whole group. So it matches ha, haha, hahaha. *[on screen: code]* ``` ha+ ha, haa, haaaa (ha)+ ha, haha, hahaha ``` Groups also do a second job. They capture. Whatever matched inside the brackets gets saved, so you can use it later, for example in find-and-replace. Then there's alternation, the vertical bar. It means or. So cat, bar, dog matches cat or dog. You'll usually put it inside a group. So for customer names with titles, you write a group with Mr, or Mrs, or Ms, then an optional dot, a space, and a word. *[on screen: code]* ``` (Mr|Mrs|Ms)\.? \w+ ``` *[on screen: regex101, that pattern, test string `Mrs Obi and Mr. Bello and Ms Ade`]* That matches Mrs Obi, Mr. Bello with the dot, and Ms Ade. ### Greedy vs lazy in regex *[on screen: the text "Bold and this" sits on screen. The pattern "<.+>" starts at the first "<" and its highlight runs hungrily all the way to the very last ">" at the end of the line, swallowing everything, with a little "greedy" label. Then a "?" drops in after the "+", and the highlight now stops at the first ">" it reaches, giving four small green blocks: "", "", "", "".]* By default, quantifiers in regex are greedy. That means they grab as much text as they can and still make a match. Say you want to find each tag in a bit of HTML, with a bold word and an italic word. You try angle bracket, dot plus, angle bracket, and you expect four matches. You get one. *[on screen: regex101, pattern `<.+>`, test string `Bold and this`]* The dot plus grabs everything, all the way to the last angle bracket at the end of the line, because every character in between counts as "any character". Add a question mark after the plus, and it becomes lazy. It takes as little as it can. So it stops at the first closing bracket it reaches, and you get four matches, one per tag. *[on screen: code]* ``` <.+> greedy: Bold and this (one match) <.+?> lazy: (four matches) ``` And for real HTML, use an HTML parser. Regex is fine for a quick search, but HTML has too many edge cases. ### How to read a regex, the email example *[on screen: the email regex from the opening comes back. It splits apart into labelled chunks, each chunk floating up with a short plain-English label under it, in the order she reads them. Then the chunks snap back together and slide along "ada.obi+books@mail.example.co.uk", each chunk lighting up the part of the email it matched, in a different soft colour.]* So let's read a real regex, one that checks the shape of an email address. *[on screen: code]* ``` ^[\w.+-]+@[\w-]+\.[\w.-]+$ ``` Read it from left to right, one piece at a time. The caret means start at the very beginning. Then a character class with backslash w, a dot, a plus and a dash. So any one word character, dot, plus or dash. Inside square brackets, the dot and the plus are normal characters again, so they don't need escaping. The plus after the brackets means one or more of those. That's the name part, like ada.obi+books. Then a literal at sign. Then one or more word characters or dashes, for the first part of the domain, like mail. Then backslash dot, a real dot, and one or more word characters, dots or dashes for the rest, like example.co.uk. And the dollar sign means it must end there. *[on screen: the pattern written out as a sentence. "Start. One or more of letters, digits, _ . + -. An @. One or more of letters, digits, _ -. A dot. One or more of letters, digits, _ . -. End."]* So that whole line of rubbish says, some name characters, an at sign, a domain with at least one dot, and nothing else before or after. *[on screen: regex101, the pattern with these test strings, one per line, with the "m" flag on so each line is tested on its own: `ada@example.com`, `ada.obi+books@mail.example.co.uk`, `ada@`, `ada@example`, `a b@example.com`. The first two match, the last three don't.]* It's a rough check, though. Real email rules allow a lot more than this, so in real apps I'd use a proper email validator. ### Regex for validation, with a Laravel example *[on screen: a form with three fields, ISBN, phone and email, slides in. Each field has a small padlock. Typed values go into each field, and the matching regex appears beside it and slides over the value. Good values turn the padlock green. A bad ISBN, "978038547454" with only twelve digits, turns its padlock red and shakes.]* The first everyday use of regex is validation, checking that what someone typed into a form has the right shape. In our bookstore, every book has an ISBN. The modern ISBN is thirteen digits, and it starts with 978 or 979. So the pattern is caret, 97, then 8 or 9 in square brackets, then ten digits, then dollar. Thirteen digits, starting with 978 or 979, and nothing else. *[on screen: regex101, pattern `^97[89]* \d{10}$`, test strings `9780385474542` (matches) and `978038547454` (doesn't, it's only twelve digits)] If you're using Laravel, for example, there's a regex validation rule. *[on screen: code]* ``` $request->validate([ 'isbn' => ['required', 'regex:/^97[89]\d{10}$/'], 'phone' => ['nullable', 'regex:/^\+?\d{10,15}$/'], 'email' => ['required', 'email'], ]); ``` The pattern has a slash at each end, because Laravel passes it to PHP's preg_match function, which needs them. The phone rule is an optional plus sign, then ten to fifteen digits. Notice the rules are in an array instead of one string with vertical bars between them. Laravel's docs warn that a vertical bar inside your regex can be mistaken for the bar between rules, so an array is safer. And for email, Laravel has an email rule that checks against the actual email standards, and that's a better check than anything I'd write myself. These patterns only check the shape. The ISBN regex can't tell you if the check digit is right, and the phone regex can't tell you if the number exists. ### Regex in find and replace, and for searching logs *[on screen: part one, a list of authors written "Achebe, Chinua" and "Adichie, Chimamanda Ngozi". The pattern highlights the surname in one colour (group 1) and the first names in another (group 2). Then the two coloured blocks swap places with a smooth slide, and the comma disappears, leaving "Chinua Achebe" and "Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie". Part two, a scrolling wall of log lines in grey. A search bar types the grep pattern, and only the ERROR and CRITICAL lines light up red and slide forward, while the rest fade.]* The second everyday use of regex is find-and-replace in your code editor. In VS Code, for example, the dot-star button in the find box turns on regular expressions. Say you have a list of authors written surname first, like "Achebe, comma, Chinua", and you want "Chinua Achebe". *[on screen: code]* ``` Find: ^([^,]+), (.+)$ Replace: $2 $1 ``` The first group is everything that isn't a comma, so that's the surname. Then a comma and a space, and the second group is everything else, the first names. In the replace box, dollar 2 and dollar 1 mean what those groups captured, so you're swapping them. And "Adichie, Chimamanda Ngozi" becomes "Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie", with both first names. *[on screen: VS Code find and replace with regex on, run on the author list]* The third everyday use is searching logs. If you're using Laravel, for example, every line in your log file looks like this. *[on screen: code]* ``` [2026-10-26 09:14:03] production.ERROR: Payment failed for order 1042 [2026-10-26 09:15:10] production.INFO: Order 1043 created [2026-10-26 09:20:44] production.CRITICAL: Database connection lost ``` grep, a command-line search tool, can pull out only the errors. *[on screen: code]* ``` grep -E "\.(ERROR|CRITICAL):" storage/logs/laravel.log ``` That says, a real dot, then ERROR or CRITICAL, then a colon. The minus capital E tells grep to use extended regex, so the brackets and the vertical bar work as you'd expect. One warning. grep has its own older flavor of regex, and backslash d doesn't work in it the way it does in PHP. So in grep, use 0 to 9 in square brackets for a digit. *[optional line: Speaking of grep, that name is the reason regex is everywhere today, and the story of where it came from is short.]* ### Where regular expressions came from *[on screen: a simple timeline slides in from the left, with a dot for each year. 1951 shows a hand-drawn network of circles labelled "Kleene, regular events". 1956 shows a book cover outline labelled "Automata Studies". 1968 shows an old terminal with "QED" and "Thompson". 1973 shows a terminal prompt typing "grep". Then a final dot labelled "today" fills with logo-free icons of a code editor, a form and a log file.]* Regular expressions started as maths, long before anyone typed one into a computer. In 1951, a mathematician called Stephen Kleene wrote a research memo at the RAND Corporation about a mathematical model of nerve cells. He described the patterns of input those models could recognise, and called them regular events. The star we use for "zero or more" is often called the Kleene star, after him. In 1968, Ken Thompson, who later co-created Unix, published a paper called "Regular Expression Search Algorithm", and built regular expressions into a text editor called QED. Then they went into ed, the editor he wrote for early Unix. In ed, if you wanted to print every line that matched a pattern, you typed g, slash, your regular expression, slash, p. Global, regular expression, print. g, r, e, p. Brian Kernighan, who worked with Thompson at Bell Labs, tells the story like this. A colleague, Lee McMahon, wanted to search the Federalist Papers, which were too big for ed. He asked Thompson, went home, and came back the next day to a program called grep. grep shipped with Unix in 1973, and that's a big part of why regex ended up in so many tools. And the joke about regex is old too. In 1997, a programmer called Jamie Zawinski wrote this. *[on screen: "Some people, when confronted with a problem, think 'I know, I'll use regular expressions.' Now they have two problems." Jamie Zawinski, 1997]* ### Using AI to write regex, and why you still need to read it *[on screen: a chat bubble pops up with "write me a regex for..." and a regex streams back into a second bubble. The regex drops onto a test bench with two trays labelled "should match" and "should NOT match". Example strings slide across the regex one by one, and each one lands in the right tray with a tick, until one bad string lands in the wrong tray with a red cross. Then, for the backtracking part, the pattern "(a+)+$" sits over a line of a's ending in "b", and a counter of "attempts" climbs faster and faster while a CPU bar fills red.]* These days, a lot of us don't write regex from scratch anymore. We ask AI. I think that's fine, because AI is good at regex. But you still need to be able to read it, for three reasons. The first reason is that it can look right and still be wrong. So paste it into regex101 with two lists, things that should match and things that should not. The second list is where the bugs usually show up. For the ISBN, that's twelve digits, fourteen digits, and a number starting with 977. *[on screen: regex101, the ISBN pattern with the "m" flag on and a should-match / should-not-match list in the test string box]* The second reason is flavors. PHP, JavaScript and Python each have their own flavor of regex. The basics work the same in all three, but the advanced features can differ. So tell the AI your language, and pick the same flavor on regex101, PCRE2 for PHP and ECMAScript for JavaScript. The third reason is speed. When a regex fails partway through a match, the engine can go back and try another way. That's called backtracking. Some patterns give it so many ways to try that the work explodes. The pattern on screen, run on a long line of a's with a b at the end, tries a huge number of ways to split up the a's before it gives up. Every extra a roughly doubles the work. *[on screen: code]* ``` (a+)+$ on aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaab ``` That's called catastrophic backtracking. On the 2nd of July 2019, Cloudflare had a global outage for about half an hour. Their own write-up says a regular expression in one of their firewall rules backtracked so much that it used up the CPUs handling web traffic across their network. And people wrote that regex, before today's AI coding tools. So the lesson is the same whoever writes it. Someone has to read it. So if a pattern has a quantifier inside a group that also has a quantifier, test it on long, nasty input. And ask the AI to explain each piece, left to right. If the explanation doesn't match what you need, you'll catch it. So, what's the worst regex you've ever had to read? Paste it in the comments, and let's read it together.

script:
### Open

*[on screen: a bookstore app. A book with "€30" crossed out and "€18" next to it]*

You open a bookstore app, and a book you like used to be thirty euros, and now it's eighteen.

You feel like you just saved twelve euros, so you buy it.

But if that book had just said eighteen euros from the start, would you have bought it?

That feeling of a good deal comes from a cognitive bias, and apps are designed around biases like this every day.

So in this video, I'll explain what a cognitive bias is, and seven of them that apps use, and how good designers design around them.

### What a cognitive bias is

So what is a cognitive bias?

Your brain can't think hard about every small decision you make in a day, so it uses shortcuts.

For example, if you see a long queue in front of one food spot and nobody at the one next to it, you'll probably guess the busy one is better.

Most of the time, that shortcut works.

In 1974, two psychologists, Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman, published a famous paper about these shortcuts. They called them heuristics.

They said these shortcuts are usually useful, but sometimes they lead to errors that are systematic.

Systematic means the errors aren't random. Lots of people make the same mistake, in the same direction, in the same kind of situation.

That predictable error is what we call a cognitive bias.

*[on screen: heuristic = a mental shortcut / cognitive bias = the predictable mistake the shortcut makes]*

Years later, Kahneman wrote a book called Thinking, Fast and Slow.

In it, he used two names from the psychologists Keith Stanovich and Richard West. System 1 is fast and automatic, like reading a sign without trying. System 2 is slow and effortful, like working out seventeen times twenty-four.

They're a way to describe two kinds of thinking, and they aren't two separate parts of your brain.

Kahneman links most of these biases to the fast kind of thinking, when you decide before you've really thought about it.

You've probably heard of confirmation bias, where you look for things that agree with what you already believe. I covered that one in my video on how to think clearly.

I care about this as a Human-Computer Interaction student because every app makes choices for you, so every design meets these shortcuts, whether the designer planned it or not.

### Anchoring bias

The first cognitive bias is anchoring.

Anchoring is when the first number you see pulls your judgement towards it, even when that number has nothing to do with the question.

In that same 1974 paper, Tversky and Kahneman spun a wheel of fortune in front of people. The wheel was set up to stop on either 10 or 65.

Then they asked people what percentage of countries in the United Nations were in Africa.

The people who saw 10 gave a typical answer of about 25 percent, and the people who saw 65 gave about 45 percent.

*[on screen: wheel lands on 10, typical guess about 25% / wheel lands on 65, typical guess about 45%]*

A random number from a wheel moved their answers by about twenty points.

In apps, the anchor is usually the crossed-out price.

In our bookstore, thirty becomes the anchor, and eighteen feels cheap next to it.

Designing around anchoring starts with honest anchors.

In the EU, when a shop announces a price reduction, the old price it shows has to be the lowest price it charged in the 30 days before the reduction.

And for you as a shopper, the question to ask is the one from the start. Would I pay eighteen euros for this if I had never seen thirty?

### The default effect

The second cognitive bias is the default effect.

The default effect is when people stick with whatever option is already chosen for them.

The most famous study on this is about organ donation.

In 2003, Eric Johnson and Daniel Goldstein compared European countries where you have to sign up to be a donor, which is opt-in, with countries where you're counted as a donor unless you say no, which is opt-out.

Kahneman describes their numbers in his book as close to 100 percent in Austria, which is opt-out, and only 12 percent in Germany, right next door.

*[on screen: Germany (opt-in) about 12% / Austria (opt-out) close to 100%]*

They also ran an online experiment, where the only thing that changed was the default.

With opt-in, 42 percent agreed to be donors. With opt-out, 82 percent stayed donors.

One careful note here. Those numbers are about consent, meaning who is counted as a donor. Actual donations went up by much less. In their own analysis, opt-out countries had around 16 percent higher donation rates.

Changing which box is already ticked changed what people ended up with.

In apps, defaults are everywhere.

Notifications, auto-renew and data sharing usually start switched on, in settings most people never open.

Defaults can also help people, like a savings plan that signs you up unless you say no.

So as a designer, the question I'd ask is simple. If most people never change this setting, is the default the one that's best for them?

### The framing effect

The third cognitive bias is the framing effect.

The framing effect is when the same information makes you decide differently, depending on how it's worded.

In 1988, Irwin Levin and Gary Gaeth showed people ground beef.

For some people, it was labelled 75 percent lean. For others, it was labelled 25 percent fat.

That's the same beef. 75 percent lean means 25 percent fat.

But people rated the beef better when it was described as 75 percent lean.

*[on screen: "75% lean" and "25% fat" side by side, with an equals sign between them]*

Apps use framing all the time.

A yearly plan that says "save 17 percent" sounds better than one that says "pay 100 euros today", even when it's the same plan.

Designing around framing matters most when the decision is important, like health, money or privacy.

So for those, I think a good design shows both sides, like the yearly saving and what you pay today.

That way, the wording isn't making the decision for the person.

### The availability heuristic

The fourth one is the availability heuristic.

The availability heuristic is when you judge how common something is by how easily examples come to your mind.

Tversky and Kahneman tested it with letters.

They asked people whether the letter K shows up more often as the first letter of English words, or as the third letter.

Most people said the first letter, because words like kitchen and king come to mind easily, and words like ask and make don't.

But in normal English text, K shows up more often in the third position.

*[on screen: K first: kitchen, king, kind / K third: ask, make, like, take]*

So the thing that's easier to remember feels more common, even when it isn't.

In apps, one long, scary review with photos sticks in your mind much more than four hundred short good ones.

Designing around availability means showing the whole picture next to the vivid story.

For example, a good review section shows how all the ratings are spread out, from one star to five, right above the reviews.

### Social proof

The fifth one is social proof.

Social proof is when we decide what to do by looking at what other people are doing.

It's the queue at the food spot again, and the psychologist Robert Cialdini made the term famous.

In 2008, Noah Goldstein, Robert Cialdini and Vladas Griskevicius tested it in a hotel.

They put cards in the rooms asking guests to reuse their towels. With a card about saving the environment, about 35 percent did.

Another card said that almost 75 percent of guests reuse their towels. With that card, about 44 percent reused them.

*[on screen: "help save the environment" about 35% / "most guests reuse their towels" about 44% / "guests who stayed in this room" about 49%]*

And in a second experiment, the card that said "the guests who stayed in this room" did best of all, at about 49 percent.

The closer the other people were to you, the stronger it worked.

In apps, social proof is the star rating, the "bestseller" badge, "most popular" on a pricing plan, and "2,000 people bought this".

Designing around it means only using real numbers.

Fake reviews and made-up "twelve people are looking at this" messages are dark patterns, and in the EU and the UK, regulators have gone after them.

### Loss aversion and scarcity

The sixth one is loss aversion.

Loss aversion is when losing something feels worse than gaining the same thing feels good.

Losing ten euros hurts more than finding ten euros makes you happy.

It's part of Kahneman and Tversky's prospect theory from 1979. They later estimated that losses weigh about twice as much as gains, although newer research shows that number changes a lot between people and situations.

*[optional line: If you've ever opened Duolingo at 11:58 pm just to save your streak, this one is about you.]*

Duolingo is the best example I know. Their own blog says the streak works partly through loss aversion. Once you have a long streak, you don't want to lose it.

They also wrote that learners who reach a 7-day streak are 3.6 times more likely to complete their course.

And they added a streak freeze, which lets you skip a day. I think that's good design, because the streak helps you learn, and the freeze stops it from punishing you for one bad day.

*[on screen: a streak counter at 47 days, with a small streak freeze icon]*

Scarcity is close to loss aversion. When something looks rare, we want it more.

In 1975, Stephen Worchel and his colleagues gave people cookies from a jar. When the jar had only two cookies, people rated the cookies as more desirable than when the jar had ten.

In apps, scarcity is "only 2 rooms left" and the countdown timer on a deal.

When it's true, it's useful information.

When it isn't, it's pressure selling. In 2019, the UK's competition regulator got Booking.com, Expedia, Agoda and Trivago to commit to stopping it.

I made a whole video on dark patterns, including how to check if a countdown timer is fake, so I'll link it here.

### The decoy effect

The seventh cognitive bias is the decoy effect.

The decoy effect is when adding a third option that nobody really wants changes which of the other two options people pick.

It was first shown in 1982, by Joel Huber, John Payne and Christopher Puto.

The most famous example comes from Dan Ariely's book, Predictably Irrational.

He saw an offer from The Economist. Online only was 59 dollars, print only was 125, and print and online together was also 125.

Nobody wants print only, because for the same price, you get print and online.

When he gave these three options to his students, 84 percent chose print and online.

When he took the print only option away, only 32 percent chose print and online.

*[on screen: three cards. Online $59 (16%) / Print $125 (0%) / Print + online $125 (84%). Then two cards: Online $59 (68%) / Print + online $125 (32%)]*

The print only option did its job without anyone choosing it. It made print and online look like a great deal.

In our bookstore, it would be an ebook for ten euros, a paperback for twenty, and both together for twenty.

To be fair to the research, the original authors have said the decoy effect only shows up under certain conditions, for example when people are already torn between the two main options.

Designing around it means every option on the page should be one that someone might really want.

### How to use cognitive biases in design fairly

So is designing with cognitive biases manipulation?

I think you can't design without them, because every screen has a default and every price sits next to something.

In 2008, Richard Thaler and Cass Sunstein called this choice architecture, in their book Nudge. A nudge is a design that makes one choice easier, without taking any options away.

Later, Thaler gave a name to the bad version. He called it sludge.

Sludge is design that makes it harder for you to do what's good for you, like a subscription that takes one click to start and twenty minutes to cancel.

Thaler's test for a good nudge is close to this. It's open about what it's doing, it's easy to say no to, and it leaves the person better off.

*[on screen: a good nudge is open / easy to say no to / good for the person]*

That's the test I want to use on my own designs. If I'd be embarrassed to explain to the user why the screen looks the way it does, it's probably sludge.

This is the first video in a series where I explain UX concepts in simple words, so tell me which concept you want next.

And tell me in the comments, which of these seven did you notice in an app this week?

script:
### Open

You read a chapter, you close the book, and you feel like you know it.

Then someone asks you one question about it, and nothing comes.

Or you're halfway through explaining something, and a little voice in your head says, wait, do I really understand this?

That little voice has a name. It's called metacognition.

In this video, I'll explain what it is, why your feeling of "I know this" can be wrong, and simple ways to practise it, including when you use AI.

### What is metacognition?

Metacognition means thinking about your own thinking.

It's the part of you that notices what's going on in your own head while you learn, decide or solve a problem.

The word comes from an American psychologist called John Flavell.

In 1976, he gave an example I really like.

He wrote, "I am engaging in metacognition if I notice that I am having more trouble learning A than B."

So if you've ever noticed that maths goes in easier for you than history, that noticing is metacognition.

Then in 1979, he wrote a paper that made the idea popular, and he opened it with a study his team had done with children.

They asked preschool and primary school children to study a set of items until they were sure they could remember all of them.

The older children studied for a while, said they were ready, and usually were.

The younger children also studied for a while and said they were ready, and usually were not.

*[on screen: older children: "I'm ready" and usually were / younger children: "I'm ready" and usually were not (Flavell, 1979)]*

So both groups did the studying. The difference was in knowing when they had learned it.

And Flavell didn't think this was only a children's problem.

He wrote that there is "far too little rather than enough or too much" cognitive monitoring in this world, and that this is true for adults as well as for children.

Cognitive monitoring is the checking part. Checking whether you understand, whether you remember, and whether what you're doing is working.

### The three parts of metacognition

Researchers split metacognition up in slightly different ways, but a simple way a lot of them use has three parts.

Knowledge, monitoring and control. Some people call that last one regulation.

*[on screen: metacognition = knowledge + monitoring + control (also called regulation)]*

I'll use one example for all three. Say you're learning a new language. I did Estonian A1 at my university, so this one is close to home.

The first part is metacognitive knowledge.

That's what you know about how you learn, about the task in front of you, and about which strategies work.

For example, knowing that words you only read once don't stay with you.

The second part is monitoring. That's checking yourself while you're learning.

You look at your list of Estonian words and ask, do I really know these, or do they only look familiar because they're right in front of me?

The third part is control. That's changing what you do because of what you noticed.

So you cover the English side, you test yourself, and you spend more time on the words you got wrong.

If you skip monitoring, you never find out there's a problem.

And if you skip control, you know there's a problem and nothing changes.

### Why your feeling of "I know this" can be wrong

Every time you study something, your brain makes a quick guess about how well you've learned it.

Researchers call that guess a judgment of learning.

And that guess decides when you stop studying, and how confident you feel walking into the exam.

The problem is that the guess can be wrong.

In 2006, Henry Roediger and Jeffrey Karpicke asked students to learn short passages of text.

One group read the passage four times. Another group read it once, and then practised recalling it three times.

Then the researchers asked them how well they thought they'd remember it a week later.

The students who read it four times were the most confident.

And five minutes later, they did remember more. 83% against 71%.

But one week later, it flipped. The rereaders remembered 40%, and the group that practised recalling remembered 61%.

*[on screen: read 4 times: most confident, 83% after 5 minutes, 40% after a week / read once, recalled 3 times: least confident, 71% after 5 minutes, 61% after a week (Roediger & Karpicke, 2006)]*

So rereading made the text feel familiar, and familiar felt like knowing.

Researchers like Asher Koriat and Robert Bjork call this an illusion of competence. You feel more competent than you are, because the information keeps being right there in front of you.

The good news is that you can make your guess better.

In 1991, Thomas Nelson and John Dunlosky had people learn pairs of words, and asked them to judge how well they'd remember each pair.

When people judged straight away, they were only moderately accurate.

When they judged a little later, seeing only the first word of the pair, they were much more accurate.

So the simple version is this. Don't ask "do I know this?" while you're looking at it.

Close the book, wait a bit, and try to bring it back. What comes back is a much better answer.

### Is the Dunning-Kruger effect real?

The Dunning-Kruger effect comes up a lot when people talk about metacognition, so I want to be careful with it.

In 1999, Justin Kruger and David Dunning tested people on humour, grammar and logic.

They reported that people who scored in the bottom quarter were around the 12th percentile, and they guessed they were around the 62nd.

*[on screen: bottom quarter: scored around the 12th percentile, guessed around the 62nd (Kruger & Dunning, 1999)]*

Kruger and Dunning linked this to metacognition.

Their idea was that the skills you need to do something well are often the same skills you need to notice you're doing it badly.

That idea has been argued about a lot since.

In 2020, Gilles Gignac and Marcin Zajenkowski argued that a big part of the famous pattern is a statistical artefact.

That means the way the data is grouped and drawn can create a pattern like it, even without the effect.

Two ordinary things can do it.

First, most people rate themselves a bit above average.

Second, if you score very low on one test, part of that is usually bad luck on the day, so your guess about yourself doesn't drop as far as your score did.

Put those two together, and the bottom group looks very overconfident, even if nobody is especially blind to their own skill.

When they tested 929 people with a better method, they found the effect may be much smaller than reported before. They called it mostly an artefact, and they didn't say it's entirely one.

*[optional line: There's another side to this, and it matters.]*

On the other side, in 2021, Rachel Jansen, Anna Rafferty and Tom Griffiths tested thousands of people on grammar and logic, and their results supported the idea that low performers are less able to tell when they're right.

So as of October 2026, researchers are still arguing about this.

And the internet version, the mountain graph with "Mount Stupid" at the top, isn't in the 1999 paper at all.

What I'm comfortable saying is smaller.

How sure you feel is weak evidence of how good you are, whether you're near the bottom or near the top. Checking yourself is what tells you.

### Can metacognition be taught? What schools found

Can metacognition be taught? In schools, there's a lot of evidence on this.

The Education Endowment Foundation, or EEF, is a charity in England that gathers research on what helps children learn, and puts it in a toolkit for teachers.

As of October 2026, their toolkit lists metacognition and self-regulation at plus eight months.

That means students who got these approaches made about eight extra months of progress, on average, compared with similar students who didn't.

They describe it as high impact for very low cost, based on extensive evidence.

*[on screen: metacognition and self-regulation: +8 months, very low cost, extensive evidence (EEF Teaching and Learning Toolkit, as of October 2026)]*

You might see plus seven quoted elsewhere, from older or partner versions of the toolkit.

It's an average across many studies in schools, with teachers trained to teach it, so it isn't a promise for one person watching a YouTube video.

And EEF's guidance on this, which they updated in November 2025, talks about teaching students to plan, monitor and evaluate their learning.

### How to practise metacognition

If you want to practise metacognition yourself, the easiest place to start is three sets of questions. One set for before, one for during, and one for after.

Before you start, you plan.

What exactly am I being asked to do? What do I already know about this? How will I learn it, and how will I know I've got it?

While you're working, you monitor.

Can I say this without looking? Which part is confusing me? Is what I'm doing working, or am I only busy?

After, you evaluate.

What worked? What didn't? What will I do differently next time?

*[on screen: PLAN: what am I asked to do? what do I already know? how will I know I've got it? / MONITOR: can I say it without looking? what's confusing me? is this working? / EVALUATE: what worked? what didn't? what will I change?]*

In 2017, Patricia Chen and her colleagues at Stanford gave students in a statistics class a short online survey, about a week to ten days before each exam.

It took about fifteen minutes. Students thought about what the exam would cover, picked which class resources they would use, wrote why each one would help, and planned how they'd use it.

Those students finished the class about a third of a letter grade higher, on average, than students who didn't get the survey.

And using more resources didn't help them. Using them more thoughtfully did.

*[optional line: The next one is my favourite, because you can try it with whatever you're learning today.]*

The next one is self-explanation. That means explaining to yourself why each step makes sense while you're learning it.

In 1989, Michelene Chi and her colleagues watched students study worked examples in physics.

The students who learned the most were the ones who kept explaining the steps to themselves.

So when you read a solution, stop at each line and ask why this step comes next, and how it connects to the one before.

The last one is called an exam wrapper. Marsha Lovett at Carnegie Mellon University has written a lot about these.

After a test comes back, you fill in a short sheet. How did I prepare? What kinds of mistakes did I make? What will I change for the next one?

To be fair, the evidence on wrappers is mixed.

In 2017, Raechel Soicher and Regan Gurung tried them in one course, and found no improvement in exam scores, final grades or metacognition.

So I'd try a wrapper as a habit, and see if it helps you.

### Metacognition, apps and AI

Metacognition is also a design question, and that's the part I care about as an HCI student.

A lot of apps are built to make things feel easy, and easy can feel like knowing.

In 2024, Lev Tankelevitch and his colleagues at Microsoft Research presented a paper at CHI, which is a big human-computer interaction conference.

It's called "The Metacognitive Demands and Opportunities of Generative AI."

Their point is that AI tools ask a lot of your metacognition.

You have to know what you want, break the task into parts, judge whether the answer is any good, and decide when to use AI at all.

One of their suggestions is that these systems "cue users to reflect on their goals and strategies via question prompts."

They also pointed out that a smooth, fluent answer can raise your confidence without making you more accurate.

In 2025, a team from Carnegie Mellon and Microsoft Research, led by Hao-Ping Lee, surveyed 319 knowledge workers about 936 real examples of using AI at work.

Higher confidence in the AI was linked to less critical thinking. Higher confidence in themselves was linked to more.

It's a survey, so it shows a link, and it can't prove that one causes the other.

*[optional line: This next part is the one I'd build myself.]*

If I were designing a study app, I'd add one small thing.

Before it shows you the answer, it asks, how sure are you?

And over time, it shows you how often your "very sure" was right.

I use AI every day, so this is what I would tell you.

Before you ask AI, write down what you already know and what you think the answer is.

Then compare. The gap between your answer and the AI's answer shows you what you didn't know, and that's usually the part worth learning.

If you watched my video on curiosity, it's the same idea. Let the question sit with you for a moment before you hand it over.

So tell me in the comments, when you study, do you reread or do you test yourself?

script:
### Open

Your phone says it's connected to Wi-Fi, and nothing loads.

Or your Wi-Fi is fast in the living room, and in your bedroom it can barely open a page.

I'm not a network engineer, and this video isn't for network engineers.

It's for everyone who uses the internet every day, and I think there are some networking basics every one of us should know.

So I'll name all of them quickly first, and then explain the ones that matter most with everyday examples.

And at the end, I'll show you why your Wi-Fi gets slow, and the simple fixes that work.

### Every networking word in this video, in one line each

These are the networking words you'll hear in this video, with what each one means in one line.

*[on screen: each word appears as she says it, building a list]*

Wi-Fi is the radio connection between your device and your router.

Your router runs the network inside your home.

Your modem connects your home to the line coming in from your internet provider.

Your internet service provider, or ISP, is the company you pay for internet.

2.4 gigahertz and 5 gigahertz are the two main radio bands your Wi-Fi uses.

An IP address is the address a device uses so data can find it.

DHCP is how your router gives out those addresses automatically.

NAT is how all the devices in your home share one public address.

A MAC address is an ID for your device's network chip, used on the local network.

DNS turns names like youtube.com into IP addresses.

A port tells a computer which program a message is for.

HTTPS encrypts what goes between your browser and a website.

A VPN sends your traffic through another company's server, inside an encrypted tunnel.

Ethernet is the cable option, and it's usually faster and steadier than Wi-Fi.

Bandwidth, the thing we call speed, is how much data can move every second.

Latency, or ping, is how long a message takes to get somewhere and back.

And a firewall decides which connections are allowed in and out.

Some of these you only need to recognise.

The rest of this video explains the ones that affect you every day.

### Wi-Fi vs internet (router, modem and your ISP)

Wi-Fi and the internet are two different things, and that's why your phone can say "connected, no internet."

Think of your home as a house on a street.

Wi-Fi is like the hallways inside the house.

It connects your phone, your laptop and your TV to the router, and it stops around your walls.

The router is like the receptionist at the front desk.

It knows every device in the house, and it passes messages in and out for them.

The modem is the front gate.

It connects your house to the fibre, cable or phone line coming in from outside.

And your internet service provider, the company you pay every month, owns the road from your gate to the rest of the internet.

*[on screen: phone, laptop, TV / Wi-Fi (hallways) / router (receptionist) / modem (front gate) / ISP (the road) / the internet]*

In a lot of homes, the router and the modem are inside one box from your provider, so it looks like one thing.

And if you use a MiFi, one of those small pocket routers, that little device is the router and the modem together, and it connects to a mobile network instead of a cable.

So when your phone says "connected, no internet," your phone can reach the router, and the hallway is fine.

The problem is further out, at the modem, the line, or your provider.

One quick test helps here.

If every device in the house has lost internet, the problem is probably the router, the modem or your provider, and restarting the router and modem is the first thing to try.

If only one device has the problem, look at that device first.

### 2.4 GHz vs 5 GHz Wi-Fi

Most Wi-Fi routers today send Wi-Fi on two radio bands, 2.4 gigahertz and 5 gigahertz, and some newer ones add 6 gigahertz.

You might see them as two network names, like "Home" and "Home-5G."

That 5G means 5 gigahertz, and it has nothing to do with 5G mobile data.

2.4 gigahertz reaches further and gets through walls better, but it's slower.

5 gigahertz is faster, but it has a shorter range, and walls and floors weaken it more.

It's a bit like music from your neighbour's party.

Through the wall, you hear the bass, but you can't make out the singer's words.

Lower frequencies get through walls better, and that's the same reason 2.4 travels further.

*[on screen: 2.4 GHz, further, through walls, slower / 5 GHz, faster, shorter range]*

2.4 gigahertz also gets crowded.

Your neighbours' Wi-Fi uses it, Bluetooth devices use it, and microwave ovens work in that same part of the airwaves.

Cisco has a guide on Wi-Fi interference that says a microwave running near your router or your device can slow the Wi-Fi down a lot.

So when you're close to the router, 5 gigahertz is usually the better one.

When you're far away, 2.4 might be the one that keeps working.

A lot of routers now put both bands under one name and move your devices between them for you, and Apple recommends doing exactly that, one name for all the bands.

### What is an IP address? (public vs private)

An IP address is the address a device uses so data can find it on a network.

Every message on the internet carries the address it's going to and the address it came from, the same way a letter does.

And your devices have two kinds of IP address.

The private one is like a room number inside your house.

Your router gives one to each device, and at home it usually starts with 192.168 or 10.

These addresses only work inside your home network, and the same numbers are used in millions of other homes.

The public one is like your house's street address.

That's the one websites see, and in most homes, every device in the house shares it.

You can see both of yours right now.

Search "what is my IP" on Google, and the number you see is your public address.

Then open your phone's Wi-Fi settings, tap the network you're on, and you'll see a private one, something like 192.168.1.23.

*[on screen: Google "what is my IP" result next to a phone's Wi-Fi details screen showing 192.168.x.x. Take your own screenshots and blur the public one.]*

On a laptop, you can see the private one too.

*[optional]*

*[on screen: code]*

```
Windows:  ipconfig
Mac:      ipconfig getifaddr en0
```

The private address comes from something called DHCP.

When you join a Wi-Fi network, your router gives your device an address for a while, a bit like a hotel receptionist giving you a room key when you check in.

That's why you never have to type one in yourself.

The reason we have private and public addresses at all is that the original kind of IP address, IPv4, only has about 4.3 billion of them, and that isn't enough for every device on earth.

The central pool of free IPv4 addresses ran out in February 2011.

The newer version, IPv6, has far more addresses, and in March 2026, for the first time, just over half of the people reaching Google did it over IPv6, according to the Internet Society's Pulse.

### What is NAT? (how your home shares one IP address)

NAT, which stands for network address translation, is how all the devices in your home share one public IP address.

Picture your router as the receptionist at the front desk of your house again.

Your laptop wants a video from YouTube, so it hands the request to the receptionist.

The receptionist crosses out your laptop's room number, writes the house's street address on it, and sends it out.

Then it writes a line in its notebook, saying the laptop asked YouTube for this.

When YouTube replies to the street address, the receptionist checks the notebook and takes the reply to your laptop's room.

*[on screen: a notebook page / laptop, room 23, asked YouTube / phone, room 41, asked Instagram / TV, room 12, asked Netflix]*

Your phone and your TV are doing the same thing at the same time, and the notebook keeps all their replies apart.

One side effect is that a stranger on the internet usually can't start a conversation with your laptop directly, because the receptionist has no line in the notebook saying which room it's for.

That helps, but NAT wasn't designed as security, so your router's firewall and its updates still matter.

### Mobile data vs Wi-Fi (and why your IP address changes)

When you switch your phone from Wi-Fi to mobile data, your traffic leaves through a different gate.

On Wi-Fi, your phone talks to your router, and everything goes out through your home internet.

On mobile data, your phone talks to a cell tower, and everything goes out through your mobile network.

That's why your public IP address changes when you switch.

Try it.

Search "what is my IP" on Wi-Fi, then turn Wi-Fi off and search again on mobile data, and you'll get two different addresses.

Many mobile networks also share one public address between lots of their customers.

It's the same NAT idea from the house, on a much bigger scale, and it's called carrier-grade NAT.

So the address a website sees when you're on mobile data could be shared with many strangers on the same network, and it can change from time to time, which is normal.

### What is a MAC address?

A MAC address is an ID for your device's network chip, and it's used on the local network, like your home Wi-Fi or the café Wi-Fi.

If your IP address is your room number in the house, the MAC address is like the name tag your device wears.

The router uses it to tell the devices on the network apart.

It's written as six pairs of letters and numbers, something like A4:83:E7:2B:91:0C.

*[on screen: example only, A4:83:E7:2B:91:0C]*

Your MAC address doesn't travel out to the websites you visit.

It stays on the local network you're connected to.

But whoever runs that network can see it, and if your phone used the same MAC address on every network, it could be used to recognise your phone as you move between them.

That's why iPhones, since iOS 14, use something Apple calls a private Wi-Fi address.

Your phone shows a different MAC address to each network, and Apple says it's there to reduce that kind of tracking.

Newer Android phones do something similar by default.

So if you've seen "Private Wi-Fi Address" in your settings, that's what it is, and for most people it's fine to leave it on.

### What is DNS? (and ports)

DNS, the domain name system, turns website names into IP addresses.

Computers find each other with IP addresses, but people remember names.

So when you type youtube.com, your device first asks a DNS server for the IP address of youtube.com, and then it connects to that address.

It's like the contacts on your phone.

You tap "Mum," your phone dials the number, and you never have to remember the number yourself.

Usually your internet provider runs the DNS server your devices use, unless you've changed it to one like Cloudflare's 1.1.1.1 or Google's 8.8.8.8.

*[on screen: youtube.com, DNS, 142.250.x.x (example)]*

When DNS isn't working, it can look like the whole internet is down, even when your connection is fine, because your device can't turn any name into an address.

I walked through DNS step by step in my video on what happens when you type a URL and press enter, so watch that one if you want the full journey.

Ports get one line here.

If an IP address is like a company's phone number, a port is like the extension, and it tells the computer which program the message is for.

Secure websites use port 443, and your browser adds it for you, so you never type it.

And if you're a developer, my video on what happens when you send an API request follows one request from your app all the way to a server and back.

### What the HTTPS padlock means

HTTPS is the "https" at the start of a web address, and it means the connection between your browser and the website is encrypted.

Encrypted means scrambled, so anyone in the middle, like the café Wi-Fi owner or your internet provider, can't read the pages you open, the passwords you type, or your card details.

According to the Electronic Frontier Foundation, the EFF, they can usually still see which website you're on and when you visited.

They can't see the specific pages, or what you send.

For years, browsers showed a padlock for this, and a lot of people read it as "this website is safe."

In 2023, Google said that in its own research from 2021, only 11% of study participants correctly understood what the lock icon meant.

Google also said the lock icon doesn't show whether a website is trustworthy, and Chrome replaced it with a different icon from Chrome 117.

*[on screen: "only 11% of study participants correctly understood the precise meaning of the lock icon" (Chromium Blog, May 2023)]*

The FTC, the US consumer protection agency, warns that scammers create fake websites and encrypt them to make you think they're safe.

So the padlock tells you nobody in the middle can read what you send.

It tells you nothing about who is on the other end, and a fake bank website can have one too.

Before you type a password, check the website's name, letter by letter.

### Is public Wi-Fi safe?

Public Wi-Fi, at a café, an airport or a hotel, is a lot safer than it used to be, because most websites and apps now encrypt their traffic.

The FTC's advice now says that connecting through a public Wi-Fi network is usually safe, for that reason.

What's left are a few risks you can avoid.

The first one is a fake network.

Someone can set up a hotspot with a name like "Airport Free WiFi" and wait for people to join.

People call this an "evil twin," and the Florida Attorney General's office warned people about it in 2024.

So ask the staff for the exact network name before you join.

The second one is a sign-in page that asks for too much.

If a Wi-Fi sign-in page asks for your email password or your card details, close it.

The third one is a website without HTTPS, because what you type there isn't encrypted.

*[on screen: fake network names / sign-in pages asking for passwords / sites without https]*

A few habits cover most of the rest.

Turn on two-factor authentication for your important accounts, and keep your phone updated, which is also what the FTC recommends.

If you need to do your banking and you don't trust the network, switch to mobile data for those few minutes.

And turn off auto-join for networks you only used once.

### What a VPN does and doesn't do

A VPN, a virtual private network, puts your internet traffic in an encrypted tunnel to a VPN company's server, and your traffic goes out to the internet from there.

So the café Wi-Fi owner, or your internet provider, can see that you're connected to a VPN, and not much else.

And websites see the VPN server's IP address and location instead of yours.

That's why people use VPNs to look like they're browsing from another country.

There are also things a VPN doesn't do.

The EFF puts it plainly: "A VPN is not a tool for anonymity."

If you're logged into Google or Instagram, they still know it's you, and cookies can still follow you around.

The VPN company can see the traffic your internet provider used to see, so you're moving your trust from one company to another, and the EFF warns that a VPN provider could sell that information, just like an internet provider could.

A VPN also won't stop you from typing your password into a fake website, or from downloading something harmful.

*[on screen: a VPN hides your browsing from the Wi-Fi owner and your ISP, and changes your IP / it doesn't make you anonymous, stop fake websites, or hide you from the VPN company]*

With free VPN apps, be extra careful.

The FTC suggests checking an app's permissions, and whether it shares your information with other companies, before you install it.

In my opinion, a VPN is useful on networks you don't trust, or when you want to hide your browsing from your provider.

For everyday browsing at home, HTTPS is already doing the encryption part for most websites.

### Why your Wi-Fi is slow (and simple fixes)

When your Wi-Fi is slow, it usually comes down to four things.

The first one is distance, because Wi-Fi gets weaker the further you are from the router.

The second one is what's in the way.

Thick concrete walls, brick, metal and even big mirrors weaken the signal, and a router hidden in a cupboard or behind the TV is in a bad spot.

The third one is interference.

That's your neighbours' Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, and microwaves, and Ofcom, the UK's communications regulator, also tells people to keep the router away from cordless phones, halogen lamps, TVs and dimmer switches.

The fourth one is too many devices.

Everything on your Wi-Fi shares the same radio, so they take turns, and Ofcom points out that phones and tablets often use the internet in the background.

*[optional line: So if your Wi-Fi is slow right now, try these as I go through them.]*

Here are the fixes, starting with the easiest.

First, restart the router and the modem.

Second, move the router somewhere central, high up and out in the open, away from the TV and the microwave.

Third, when you're close to the router, use 5 gigahertz.

Fourth, plug in a cable for things that don't move, like a TV or a desktop computer, because Ofcom says a wired connection usually gives you faster speeds than Wi-Fi.

Fifth, disconnect devices you're not using, and don't start big downloads during an important video call.

And if your home is big or has lots of walls, a mesh Wi-Fi system, which is a few routers working together as one network, can cover the rooms one router can't reach.

*[on screen: restart / move the router / 5 GHz up close / cable for things that don't move / fewer devices / mesh for big homes]*

To find out whether the problem is your Wi-Fi or your internet, run a speed test standing right next to the router, or on a cable.

If it's slow even there, the problem is your plan or your provider, so call them.

If it's fast next to the router and slow in your room, the problem is your Wi-Fi, and the fixes above are the ones to try.

One last thing that confuses a lot of people.

Internet speeds are measured in megabits per second, but downloads show megabytes, and there are 8 bits in a byte.

So a 100 megabit connection downloads at about 12.5 megabytes a second at best, and nothing is wrong with it.

*[on screen: 100 Mbps ÷ 8 = about 12.5 MB/s]*

So tell me in the comments, which room in your house has the worst Wi-Fi, and what's between it and your router?
